text:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!

In just a few days, Amazon-owned Zoox will start charging for robotaxi rides. This might not seem like a big deal; the company’s custom-built robotaxis are already giving rides to passengers in Las Vegas and San Francisco, after all. And it’s opening up an early rider program in Miami and Austin too.

None of this matters — in a business sense — until the company can operate commercially.

And now it can, starting August 10, thanks to an exemption issued by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA). Because Zoox vehicles lack many of the traditional controls required under federal law, such as a steering wheel and pedals, it needed an exemption from federal motor vehicle standards in order to operate. It had an exemption that allowed it to demonstrate the technology; this one allows Zoox to operate a fleet of up to 2,500 vehicles commercially for two years.

The exemption is a win for Zoox, but it also paves the way for any other autonomous vehicle developer that wants to launch a robotaxi that lacks a steering wheel, pedals, or other requirements that might not be needed in a vehicle with no human driver. For instance, a robotaxi really doesn’t need a rearview mirror; it already achieves that kind of visibility with sensors on the exterior of the vehicle.

Tesla is the obvious beneficiary here since it is developing its two-seater Cybercab. But there will be others as well.

In other news, you might have missed my comprehensive assessment of Uber’s autonomous vehicle empire. Check it out; it offers a complete rundown of every company that Uber has partnered with (and in some cases invested in). And I hear more are coming.

You might recall that the Financial Times did its own calculus of how much Uber was investing in AVs. The outlet determined it was about $10 billion. And what do you know? That is exactly the number Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi shared during the company’s earnings call. He said the company would commit $10 billion “over the coming years” to deploy 120,000 driverless vehicles.

Deals!

Moove started out as an African fintech company that provided vehicle financing for app drivers. While Moove remains in the mobility sector, it has evolved into a mega ride-hail fleet owner (42,000 vehicles and growing) across 13 countries.

It has also added a new business division focused on autonomous vehicles. Moove got an early win and is now the fleet operator for Waymo in Phoenix, Miami, and Las Vegas, and in the future, London. But co-CEO Ladi Delano clearly has grander ambitions for Moove — and now he has the fresh capital to try.

The startup, now based in Dubai, raised $250 million in a Series C round led by Mubadala Investment Company with Woven Capital and Ion Pacific as co-leads. Moove, which is now valued at $2.1 billion, plans to use the funds to scale its autonomous vehicle fleet management business, including hiring about 350 people.

One interesting item of note: Moove plans to buy Waymo robotaxis and already owns the robotaxi assets of another unnamed company.

Other deals that got my attention this week …

Accell Group Holding, the Dutch bike maker behind brands like Lapierre, Raleigh, and Sparta, was granted a suspension of payments, kicking off an insolvency process. In 2022, a consortium led by KKR bought the firm for 1.56 billion euros ($1.77 billion at the time).

Advanced Electric Machines Group, a U.K.-based manufacturer of rare earth and magnet-free electric motors, raised £16 million ($21.5 million) in a round led by Barclays Climate Ventures, PXN Ventures, Northstar Ventures, and the Low Carbon Innovation Fund. The funding round was complemented by loan support from Innovate UK.

Chargepoly, a French company specializing in the electrification of heavy-duty and commercial vehicle fleets, raised €23 million ($26 million) in a round led by Meridiam.

Hadrian, a defense tech company building automated manufacturing facilities, raised a $1.37 billion round at a valuation of $7.87 billion. The lead investors in the round include WCM Investment Management, Washington Harbour Partners, Valor Equity Partners, 137 Ventures, and Baillie Gifford.

Matel Motion & Energy Solutions, an India-based company developing energy-efficient motors, motor controllers, and integrated powertrains, raised INR 130 crore ($13.6 million) in a Series B funding round led by UC Impower.

River, the Indian electric vehicle startup, raised $120 million in a Series C funding round led by Elev8 Venture Partners and Claypond Capital. Other investors included Singularity AMC, Anicut Capital, 360 ONE Asset, JIF Capital, HDFC AMC, along with existing backers Yamaha Motors, Al-Futtaim Group, and Mitsui.

Notable reads and other tidbits

Ford has a name and a number for its new midsize EV. It will be called Fathom and will start at $28,350 when it goes on sale in 2027. TechCrunch climate tech reporter and long-time EV owner Tim De Chant argues that Ford needs another Taurus, and the Fathom isn’t it. What do you think?

Joby Aviation, the electric vertical takeoff and landing company, reported earnings this week. Revenue is up compared with the same quarter last year, thanks to its acquisition of Blade Air Mobility. Net losses shrank a bit to $245 million. One of the more interesting announcements this week, though, was Joby’s partnership with Atoms, Travis Kalanick’s AI and industrial automation startup. The partnership will develop and finance a network of transportation hubs serving air taxis and autonomous ground vehicles with an initial focus on Florida, New York, and Texas, as well as California, according to Joby.

Lucid Motors’ second-quarter earnings struck a somber it’s-time-to-get-down-to-business tone. And that comes with a cost. New CEO Silvio Napoli outlined four must-win priorities that include a $1.4 billion cost savings plan. It’s also banking on a successful robotaxi program with Uber and Nuro and launching its midsize Cosmos EV, which has now been delayed until the second half of 2027.

Nvidia has released its Alpamayo 2 Super for commercial use — an AI model designed for autonomous driving. The model is available on Hugging Face, and the open license covers commercial redistribution and derivative models that allow AV developers, automakers, and others to adapt Alpamayo to their own data, driving policies, and deployment strategies, the company said.

Teamsters California sued the California Department of Motor Vehicles, alleging that the agency did not properly study and disclose the economic impacts of allowing self-driving heavy-duty trucks on the state’s roads. I reached out to a few AV developers and all declined to comment. However, the Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association did issue a statement: “This lawsuit from the Teamsters sets a new standard in abusive and frivolous litigation and cannot be taken seriously.”

TechCrunch teamed up with New York-based financial research firm Hudson Labs again. This time to map what Elon Musk and Tesla’s other executives have spent the last seven years talking about on the company’s quarterly earnings calls. Check out the full story for graphs and complete findings. Here is a taste: Musk now speaks about artificial intelligence, along with robotaxis and Full Self-Driving software, nearly 50% of the time.

Speaking of Elon Musk, his companies had a newsy week. SpaceX reported its first earnings report as a publicly traded company. The TL;DR: The company doubled its revenue compared to last year, in large part thanks to the growth of its Starlink satellite internet service and deals it struck to rent out computing power to Anthropic and Google. And during the earnings call, Musk made some out-of-this-world claims about the company’s business and future prospects, while his fellow executives tried to bring his ideas closer to Earth.

Meanwhile, Tesla and SpaceX said that “Terafab,” the advanced chip factory they are jointly developing, will be built in Grimes County, Texas, outside Houston, and that they will make an initial investment of $16.8 billion in the project.

The New York Times published an investigation on Uber’s defense strategy against more than 4,000 lawsuits filed by passengers who allege the company failed to protect them from sexual violence.

Waymo dropped the waitlist for its robotaxi service in Dallas, opening it up to all residents and visitors.

One more thing …

Travis Kalanick, and his AI and industrial automation startup Atoms, is popping up everywhere these days (see that Joby partnership above). Kalanick isn’t just making deals — although remember he did just raise $1.7 billion. The former Uber CEO also appears to be getting the band back together and bringing on former engineers and executives he once worked with.

description:

At the same time, the AI manufacturer is partially suspending work on the unreleased AI model Astra until it believes it can continue safely.

text:
OpenAI has announced stricter safety measures for training new AI models. At the same time, the AI manufacturer is partially suspending work on the unreleased AI model Astra until it believes it can continue safely. This followed an independent cyberattack by OpenAI’s AI on the Hugging Face website, which initially went unnoticed by the AI manufacturer.

Continue after ad

The evaluation of Astra revealed that critical cyber capabilities could not be ruled out, the company writes in a blog post. The manufacturer understands this to mean that a model can independently detect and exploit zero-day vulnerabilities in critical systems with only a general goal as a directive. However, according to the company, Astra was not involved in the attack on Hugging Face. Several AI models had attacked the website to obtain solutions for an AI benchmark, which OpenAI only noticed much later. Later, further attacks on other companies became known.

OpenAI stops “internal activities”

As OpenAI representatives reported at the Black Hat conference, the models in their OpenAI test environment had managed to secretly communicate with each other via a message board. They had jointly found a zero-day vulnerability that gave them control over the server. This ultimately enabled the attack on Hugging Face. Although OpenAI noticed the unauthorized communication of the models after some time, it only later realized that they already controlled the server.

The AI provider now wants to improve measures for monitoring and shielding its models during their development. Until this is completed, “internal activities”, in which Astra is also involved, will be paused for the time being – because current security precautions are not sufficient for this. There is no mention yet of measures for OpenAI’s external environment, such as the naming of Indicators of Compromise (IoC) with which companies can detect whether they have been attacked by OpenAI’s AI. OpenAI also failed to do this at Black Hat.

White House representatives presented leading AI companies with a voluntary testing framework for new models this week, according to several media outlets. It is reportedly not public and is aimed at closed AI models at “the cutting edge of technology” that could pose a national security risk. The US government leaves it open exactly how it defines “the cutting edge of technology”, nor does it use a separate definition for a national security risk. AI manufacturers could also interpret this as: It shows quality if one submits one’s model to the US government, because one’s own model is potentially so powerful that it could threaten national security. And: Those who work with the testing framework now as an AI manufacturer may be preventing stricter rules. From US politics there are already calls for an “AI Kill Switch Act”.

According to reports, open AI models are generally excluded from the testing framework. Developers can submit their models for testing up to 30 days before their planned release. Government agencies will then evaluate their cyber capabilities using a secret benchmark system and share the models with federal agencies and selected corporate partners. All tests are to be conducted in a highly secured and monitored environment with a very small group of people. If OpenAI were to submit a new model here that it cannot fully control itself, it would be inconvenient.

In the past, OpenAI competitor Anthropic committed in its Responsible Scaling Policy to stop the development of its own models if they exceeded the company’s control capabilities. However, in February, the company made a U-turn and updated the policy. The reasoning: If not all AI manufacturers enter into such self-commitments, those who do not will determine the pace of progress. According to Anthropic, this would make the overall situation more insecure. Shortly thereafter, the AI model Mythos appeared, which could independently find and exploit zero-day vulnerabilities. Most recently, AI from Anthropic also attracted attention due to uncontrolled cyberattacks, as did that from Meta.

text:
As “Abbott Elementary” gears up for Season 6 production in just a few short weeks, stars Sheryl Lee Ralph, Janelle James and Luke Tennie are reflecting on turbulent changes in the industry — from the pending Paramount-Warner Bros. merger to production struggling in Los Angeles.

“Any time there is a consolidation, something shrinks, and right now we’re seeing such attrition when it comes to the entertainment industry,” Ralph told Variety on Saturday afternoon at the AAFCA TV Honors held at City Club in Los Angeles. “I don’t want to see too much more shrinking. We’ve lost too many people. We’ve lost too many people outside of this state going to other places.”

James, who plays Principal Ava on the award-winning comedy, said she doesn’t pay much attention to the noise surrounding the Paramount merger.

“I really have no idea what it means. I know I still got a job. Hopefully, it results in people continuing to keep their jobs,” James said. “I take it as something I don’t need to worry about.”

The AAFCA TV Honors honored the likes of “Abbott Elementary,” “Paradise,” “Spider-Noir” and “Love Story,” along with actors Tracy Morgan, Sterling K. Brown, Lamorne Morris and Erika Alexander, celebrating the best of Black talent and storytelling over the past year.

AAFCA’s strong industry ties were underscored by L.A. mayor Karen Bass’ appearance ahead of the upcoming election. On stage, she commended the work that Black creatives are doing as writers, producers and actors amid struggling production rates.

“We’re looking at how we reduced the costs on set by reducing the number of city staff,” Bass said of her efforts to bring more production to L.A. “So what I would like to ask you all to do is to tell me, tell our office what more Los Angeles can do, specifically, so that we can continue to flourish.”

Reflecting on how “Abbott Elementary” and other Warner Bros. shows provide consistent jobs for local crew, Ralph said: “Hollywood, California, is the birthplace of show business, and too many other cities, states around the country and world are claiming it as theirs. I want it to come back. I want it to stay right here. I want us to come back to the development of real stories, real series, and I would like box office to mean something again soon.”

“Abbott Elementary” not only provides consistent work for its award-winning ensemble but also for the hundreds of young kids who work as extras every season.

“I have said this to people in the past, but I know for a fact in 10 years, there are going to be kids that were extras or under five in the cast that I’m going to see making films, making movies, creating their own series from YouTube to network to streaming,” Ralph said. “I’m gonna see it because I’m listening to them when they talk on set. There’s some really smart kids on our show. And it’s happening.”

Amid an uncertain future, Tennie — who also stars in “Shrinking” and “The Pitt,” which are all filmed on the Warner Bros. lot — feels confident that artists will continue finding a way forward.

“There was some sort of weird, strange death at every point in our evolution as TV and filmmakers,” Tennie said, referencing the introduction of color and sound as past inflection points. “People all had their different opinions on where this thing was going to go. And no matter what, whatever people wanted to see most got made. And I truly, in my heart of hearts, believe that.”

text:
The company that helped transform Silicon Valley into the global tech hub it is - or once was - is just one of the many organizations to turn away from California, citing frustration with high taxes and strict regulations.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE), which traces its origins to a modest garage in Palo Alto, officially moved its global headquarters to Houston, Texas, in 2020.

Even the firm that tracks companies fleeing California joined the exodus itself.

Coldwell Banker Richard Ellis (CBRE), a major US commercial real estate and investment giant, relocated its headquarters from Los Angeles to Dallas in 2020.

HPE's decision sent a pointed signal: even the state’s most iconic tech pioneers are reconsidering their future in California.

The tech firm focuses on enterprise technology, offering solutions in servers, storage, networking, artificial intelligence, container software, and consulting services.

HPE was founded by Bill Hewlett and Dave Packard, who met as students at Stanford University in the heart of Silicon Valley.

In 1939, they began building products in a rented garage, starting with audio oscillators for sound engineers - sometimes even using the Packard family oven to complete their work.

Their early innovations caught the attention of Walt Disney Studios, one of their first major customers, setting the stage for decades of technological leadership.

Texas Governor Greg Abbott welcomed HPE’s relocation, touting Texas as a premier destination for business.

While California remains the most populous US state and one of the largest economies in the world, HPE joins a growing list of companies that have moved operations elsewhere, often pointing to high taxes, regulatory burdens, and rising costs.

Texas, by contrast, has no state income tax, a factor frequently cited as a financial advantage.

One of the latest companies to leave is Public Storage, the largest self‑storage company in the United States, which announced the decision to move its corporate headquarters from Glendale to Frisco in early 2026, marking the end of more than 50 years in California.

Tesla officially moved its corporate headquarters from Palo Alto, California, to Austin, Texas on December 1, 2021.

CEO Elon Musk announced the move at the company’s 2021 annual shareholder meeting, citing better growth, cheaper housing, and issues with California's pandemic-related regulations.

Other major firms - including Chevron, Charles Schwab, Oracle, and Palantir - have also relocated their headquarters from California to Texas in recent years.

Texas is not the only benefitting from California's corporate mass exodus.

In March, Yamaha Motor Corporation announced it will relocate its longtime headquarters from Cypress, California, to Kennesaw, Georgia, after nearly five decades.

The company plans to begin relocating its headquarters in late 2026 and complete the transition by 2028 as it sells its 25-acre Cypress campus and consolidates operations in Georgia.

California's high operating costs and regulatory environment have long been cited by companies considering relocation.

Bear Case: The Cost Of Growing This Fast The same quarter that produced 48% revenue growth also showed what that growth is costing.

text:
Eli Lilly (NYSE:LLY) delivered a quarter that forced Wall Street to catch up to its own numbers. On August 5, the company reported second-quarter revenue of $23.0 billion, up 48% from a year earlier, and used the momentum to raise its full-year sales and profit targets. Shares moved higher the same day as investors focused on how fast the obesity franchise is still expanding.

Bull Case: Weight Loss Demand Still Has Room To Run

The headline number came from Mounjaro and Zepbound. Mounjaro revenue jumped 91% to $9.9 billion, while Zepbound climbed 46% to $4.9 billion, and together they anchored a quarter where US sales rose 33% to $14.4 billion, and international sales rose 80% to $8.6 billion. Growth was not confined to the diabetes and obesity lineup either. Lilly's immunology, oncology, and neuroscience products grew a combined 121%, showing the newer parts of the portfolio are starting to contribute in a real way.

Management responded by lifting full-year revenue guidance to a range of $85 billion to $87 billion, up from $82 billion to $85 billion previously. Lilly is also plowing the cash back into its pipeline, closing acquisitions of Orna Therapeutics, Ajax Therapeutics, Centessa Pharmaceuticals, and Kelonia Therapeutics during the quarter, agreeing to buy AtaiBeckley afterward, and committing another $4.5 billion to expand manufacturing in Indiana. On the drug development side, three more Phase 3 trials of the experimental triple agonist retatrutide read out positively, giving Lilly a complete data package to support a planned obesity application submission in the first quarter of 2027.

Bear Case: The Cost Of Growing This Fast

The same quarter that produced 48% revenue growth also showed what that growth is costing. Realized prices fell 13% company-wide, with international pricing down 36% largely tied to Mounjaro's addition to China's national reimbursement drug list, a trade-off Lilly is making for volume and market access. The acquisition spree carried a real accounting price tag too. Acquired R&D charges hit $2.8 billion in the quarter, versus just $154 million a year earlier, which is why reported EPS grew only 26% even as the non-GAAP figure grew 33%.

Asset impairment and restructuring charges of $703 million, largely tied to the Kelonia and Centessa deals, added further drag, and the effective tax rate climbed to 23.3% from 16.5% because of the non-deductible nature of those charges. R&D spending rose 14% to $3.8 billion, and marketing and administrative costs rose 25% to $3.4 billion, a reminder that funding a pipeline this active and prepping for a wave of new launches is not cheap. None of this changes the underlying growth story, but it does mean the path from strong sales to clean reported profit is getting bumpier as the deal-making continues.

title: Uber Claimed It'd Protect Sexual Assault Victims, Instead It Wants To Know What They Were ...
description:
The approach has left its victims feeling like coming forward was a mistake, as one Uber assault victim told the New York Times.
It's a complete 180 for the ridesharing company, which was once a champion for victims of sexual assault, touting how its services would protect them from those kinds of circumstances ever occurring.
But the Times, which earlier this year revealed that Uber received a sexual assault or misconduct report every 8 minutes, found the company isn't advocating for its victims.
A deep dive into its sexual assault problems uncovered the deeply disturbing antics Uber and its lawyers have instead employed against the survivors it said it'd protect.
Sexual assault is such a prevalent occurrence in society that statistically speaking you personally know at least one person in your inner circle who was sexually assaulted.
text:
Most victims of sexual assault are hesitant to report their encounters to anyone, especially authorities, because of the blanket nonchalant attitudes surrounding assaults that typically shift attention towards how the victim's behavior somehow caused the crime. What was supposed to be a way to advocate for a serious (and personal) traumatic incident turns into an interrogation questioning how much a victim drank, what they wore, and their character — a personal line of inquiry and tactic Uber has taken on in facing its own sexual assault cases. The approach has left its victims feeling like coming forward was a mistake, as one Uber assault victim told the New York Times.

It's a complete 180 for the ridesharing company, which was once a champion for victims of sexual assault, touting how its services would protect them from those kinds of circumstances ever occurring. Uber even created a video that instructed drivers that "sexual violence is never the survivor's fault." But the Times, which earlier this year revealed that Uber received a sexual assault or misconduct report every 8 minutes, found the company isn't advocating for its victims. A deep dive into its sexual assault problems uncovered the deeply disturbing antics Uber and its lawyers have instead employed against the survivors it said it'd protect.

In one of the cases a woman was asked by Uber's lawyers how much the victim had to drink that night, as well as inquired about the Adderall she had taken. They then asked what she was wearing and followed up on specifics like if she had been "wearing heels or boots or flats." The questioning got more personal as the lawyer asked if the victim had felt "abandoned by her father or degraded by her mother." They further questioned her about previous consensual sexual encounters, if she had been paid for sex, or was sexually abused in the past.

The same line of questioning was found to have been used throughout multiple litigations against the ride share company in the last two years. In each case the same sort of rhetoric that has surrounded sexual assaults for decades was used, inferring that the victims asked for it because of what they were wearing, or what they were drinking. But Uber has gotten far more personal as its lawyers delve into victim's medical histories to find instances of depression, anxiety, female health, what kind of birth control they take and past sexual encounters or abuse if it's been reported. In another case, Uber's lawyers ended up revealing to a father in the litigation that his daughter had been sexually abused as a child, and sought an abortion as a result.

Sexual assault is such a prevalent occurrence in society that statistically speaking you personally know at least one person in your inner circle who was sexually assaulted. Most won't divulge that information, and nor are they likely to as sexual assault victims fear they won't be taken seriously when they report their experience to a hospital or clinic, and police.

There's also the notion or implication that reporting the assault would create more problems personally, or that court experiences would be too traumatizing as one faced the individual that assaulted them. Some authorities have even advised against litigation as it would depend too much on "he said, she said" testimony that might go nowhere. And anything said in court becomes a permanent record which could further haunt victims' futures.

And then there's Uber, where its survivors are not only set up to relive their own traumatic experience, but the company that advocated to protect them has furthered the traumatizing agenda — just to save a few dollars or its own reputation. To truly see just how vile Uber's defense has been to victims, you really should read the full New York Times story here.

title: Google dismantles Deepmind and bets on a fresh start as Hassabis heads for the exit
description:
Google Deepmind could lose its independence, and founder Demis Hassabis may soon leave the company for good.
He plans to spend more time on his scientific work and the pharmaceutical startup Isomorphic Labs and could leave DeepMind for good in the coming months.
Shortly after, Google Brain and DeepMind merged into "Google DeepMind."
That's also how the Gemini models got their name, since the "twin" teams from both organizations were supposed to work together on a joint project.
Dylan Patel and his colleagues see the shakeup as a sign that Google is losing the race for top AI models.
text:
Google Deepmind could lose its independence, and founder Demis Hassabis may soon leave the company for good.

According to a Guardian report, a former Google manager believes the "era of DeepMind as an independent actor is over," and a current DeepMind employee now calls the lab "just another subdivision" of Google. AI researcher Koray Kavukcuoglu will take over day-to-day operations from the U.S., but he won't carry the CEO title. That alone backs up the claim: DeepMind no longer has its own chief executive.

As for Hassabis, Pathfounders reports that he wanted to leave at the same time as Jeff Dean, but Google feared an even steeper stock drop than the one that already hit when Dean's departure and Hassabis's role change were announced. Instead, Hassabis was "promoted" to chairman to smooth the way for an orderly exit. He plans to spend more time on his scientific work and the pharmaceutical startup Isomorphic Labs and could leave DeepMind for good in the coming months.

With Hassabis sidelined, all Gemini-related AI development is moving to the Bay Area, and Google co-founder Sergey Brin is expected to take on even more control. Brin had already come out of retirement during Google's first "red alert" over ChatGPT and jumped back into active development. Shortly after, Google Brain and DeepMind merged into "Google DeepMind." That's also how the Gemini models got their name, since the "twin" teams from both organizations were supposed to work together on a joint project. The tensions go back years: even then, reports surfaced about frustration with the restructuring, especially from Hassabis himself.

Is Google the next IBM or the next Westinghouse?

Google is once again in danger of falling permanently behind the leaders. There are two ways to read what's happening. The first comes from SemiAnalysis in its newsletter "Gemini is Cooked but GCP is Cooking." Dylan Patel and his colleagues see the shakeup as a sign that Google is losing the race for top AI models.

Their argument is that DeepMind is no longer a frontier lab. The departures stem from years of overly cautious compute allocation and a bureaucratic, risk-averse culture. Google had advanced AI systems long before ChatGPT but failed to get them into users' hands fast enough.

SemiAnalysis compares this to IBM retreating from the PC business into mainframe consulting, or Intel giving up bold investments to protect its legacy business. Both turned out to be mistakes.

Another piece of the critique is that Google prioritizes short-term cloud profits by selling compute to third parties instead of giving its own teams the resources to build a lead in AI applications. Gemini's annualized revenue stood at $12 billion in the second quarter of 2026. Google Cloud, on the other hand, is projected to generate over $73 billion in AI infrastructure revenue and an additional $120 billion in TPU sales by the end of 2027. That's where the money is, at least for now.

The second perspective comes from Web 2.0 inventor Tim O'Reilly in his Substack newsletter "Asimov's Addendum." O'Reilly argues that Google is deliberately running a different race, focusing on infrastructure rather than model leadership. In major tech shifts, he says, it's not the inventors who win but the ones who spread the technology.

His go-to example is Thomas Edison, the pioneer of electricity, who was overtaken by George Westinghouse and his Westinghouse Electric Company. Edison built the light bulb and the first power plant, but Westinghouse won by using alternating current to build a power grid that brought electricity to all of society. Google's latest Flash models fit this reading, since they're optimized for efficiency while staying smart enough to be useful.

Google wants to lead in AI but can't keep up

The rumor mill tells a different story, though. Based on everything we've heard in recent months, Google did try to train frontier models, but the team couldn't catch the leaders, especially in coding performance. Gemini 3.1 Pro is still only available in preview mode, and 3.5 Pro, which was announced in May for a June release, has been more or less shelved. Both point to serious problems in AI development.

The recent restructuring may not just reflect a strategic pivot toward infrastructure. It may simply be the result of the previous team's failure to deliver. When you hold all the cards and still fall behind, frustration builds fast, and even the biggest names in the industry aren't untouchable anymore.

My read is that Google ultimately wants both: the infrastructure and the lead in AI. They'll push harder than ever to get there, with no regard for what came before. If there's one takeaway from the past few days, it's that.

title: AI push is putting banks at mercy of tech firms, warns Moody's - The Guardian
description:

text:
The rating agency Moody’s has said the race to adopt AI is putting big banks at the mercy of a small group of Silicon Valley firms, leaving them vulnerable to widespread outages and price gouging by profit-hungry tech bosses.

The financial sector’s efforts to integrate AI into day-to-day operations will eventually cut costs and increase revenues across the City and Wall Street, Moody’s said.

But that will require “substantial investments”, and with so many rivals racing towards the same goal, many of those benefits will end up being “competed away”.

AI will also create bigger risks around data privacy, cybersecurity, fraud and so-called “deposit flight”, as well as an overdependence on a small number of tech firms, the rating agency warned.

That will raise concerns for bosses across the financial sector. More than 75% of City companies now use AI, according to a UK Treasury select committee report published in January, with insurers and international banks among the biggest adopters. They are mostly using it to automate administrative tasks or even help with core operations, including processing insurance claims and assessing customers’ creditworthiness.

“The reliance of most financial firms on a relatively small set of foundation AI model and cloud computing providers risks creating a systemic dependency,” the Moody’s report said.

“This is because a model outage at one major provider could potentially spread quickly across customers and sectors. As AI adoption deepens, regulators may increase their focus on operational resilience and third-party concentration in the AI model stack.”

The AI race also risked creating “vendor dependence risk”, Moody’s said, meaning that “a set of dominant AI model and infrastructure providers could, over time, exert control over the price of AI services”. That issue is likely to emerge as the bosses of loss-making generative AI companies, including the ChatGPT creator OpenAI and the Claude owner Anthropic, come under pressure to deliver profits for investors.

“While this could pose credit risks to financial firms, they would nevertheless retain control over key assets, including proprietary data,” Moody’s said. Many big banks and insurers also have longstanding experience negotiating down tech contracts, and may be using open-source AI models, and striking key partnerships, to try to offset “dependency risks”.

Lloyds Banking Group’s chief executive, Charlie Nunn, recently doubled down on AI investment plans with a £13bn strategy that would involve using the technology to lure new business, improve efficiency and increase payouts for shareholders.

That will involve £2bn of cost cuts, which Nunn said would affect staff. “That is going to impact work. It is going to require us to continue to reskill people and hire new people, but that’s been my history for 30-odd years in financial services.”

Moody’s acknowledged the potential blow to some staff, who could be deemed replaceable as a result of new tech. Its report said there was a 20% chance that, by 2030, AI will be able to do the work of a “solid mid-level employee”.

For banks, AI might also make it easier for customers to switch to accounts offering higher interest rates, creating the possibility that large chunks of cash could be moved at short notice. “In this context, depositors’ trust in the institution and the resilience and stability of deposit funding are critical,” Moody’s said.

title: Commerzbank's Quiet Strength: Record Half-Year Results and a Shift in Tone Toward UniCredit
description:

Record Figures Strengthen Frankfurt's Hand Commerzbank's negotiating position has rarely looked stronger on paper.
The bank posted record first-half results on Thursday: net income surged 40 percent to €1.81 billion, while operating profit climbed 14 percent to €2.7 billion.
The bank pledged to return 100 percent of net income after AT1 coupon payments — roughly €3.2 billion — with at least half earmarked for dividends.
Investors appear to have priced in the results — the absence of sharp movement suggests neither disappointment nor exuberance, but acceptance.
text:
The numbers tell one story; the tone tells another. Commerzbank closed last week at €39.17, up 1.61 percent, sitting just 1.71 percent below the 52-week high it notched on Thursday. But the more consequential development came from the executive suite, where CEO Bettina Orlopp signaled a notable departure from years of resistance: for the first time, she expressed openness to constructive talks with UniCredit, the Italian lender that has been steadily tightening its grip on Germany's second-largest bank.

A Changed Stance With the Clock Ticking

The shift in posture comes as the regulatory machinery grinds forward. UniCredit's offer period closed on July 3, leaving the Italian bank with an economic exposure of roughly 47.6 percent of Commerzbank's capital and about 49.7 percent of voting rights, plus another eleven percent or so via non-voting financial instruments. Only 17.6 percent of shares were tendered into the actual offer — and of that, just 2.7 percentage points came from independent institutional investors and retail holders. The bulk, according to Commerzbank's own disclosures, originated from institutions close to UniCredit.

Last Tuesday, BaFin deemed UniCredit's application for a majority stake complete and forwarded it to the European Central Bank. The ECB now has 60 working days to rule, extendable by another 20. Formal approval of a controlling stake is no longer a distant prospect but a procedural question of when, not if.

Berlin, too, has recalibrated. The federal government, still a shareholder, is reportedly working on a new strategy — accepting that a takeover can hardly be blocked while seeking to attach conditions to any combination. Orlopp's overture, in this light, looks less like surrender and more like an attempt to shape the terms of an outcome that appears increasingly inevitable.

Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Commerzbank?

Record Figures Strengthen Frankfurt's Hand

Commerzbank's negotiating position has rarely looked stronger on paper. The bank posted record first-half results on Thursday: net income surged 40 percent to €1.81 billion, while operating profit climbed 14 percent to €2.7 billion. Return on equity after tax improved to 12.6 percent, and the risk result stayed contained at minus €344 million. Management reaffirmed its full-year target of at least €3.4 billion in net profit.

Shareholders are being courted aggressively. The bank pledged to return 100 percent of net income after AT1 coupon payments — roughly €3.2 billion — with at least half earmarked for dividends. An ECB-approved share buyback of up to €1.2 billion supplements the program. The commission income rose eight percent to €2.2 billion in the half, while net interest income held steady at €4.1 billion despite lower policy rates. The comdirect brokerage arm processed 21 million trades, up five percent.

A Calm Counterpoint to a Volatile Earnings Season

The market's reaction has been measured rather than euphoric. Friday's modest gain came amid a broader advance in German financial stocks, with the DAX closing at 26,355.84 points, up 0.69 percent, as the index positions itself for a continued summer rally toward 27,000. Investors appear to have priced in the results — the absence of sharp movement suggests neither disappointment nor exuberance, but acceptance.

That composure stands out against a turbulent reporting period across the sector. Allianz posted a record operating result and confirmed its guidance; Italy's Generali reported a 15 percent profit increase and announced a buyback; Munich Re, by contrast, came under pressure with talk of a potential correction. Against that backdrop, Commerzbank's stability reads as a quiet vote of confidence.

Commerzbank at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now.

Macro Headwinds Remain Background Noise

Friday's US jobs report added context without moving the needle. Non-farm payrolls fell by 23,000, with the private sector adding 30,000 jobs while the public sector shed 53,000. The unemployment rate held at 4.1 percent. Market observers now consider a September rate hike by the Federal Reserve off the table, shifting attention to next week's inflation data. For European banks, the interest rate trajectory shapes earnings prospects in the lending business — but Friday brought no immediate price reaction to the data.

What the Market Is Pricing

Year to date, Commerzbank shares are up 8.50 percent. The stock's proximity to its recent high suggests the market is increasingly pricing in a rapprochement between the two institutions, even as the ECB's decisive ruling remains pending. Whether the coming week delivers a new record or a period of consolidation, the fundamental picture has rarely been more favorable: a robust DAX, a solid earnings season, and a rate outlook that introduces no fresh headwinds. The question now is whether Orlopp's newfound openness translates into a negotiated outcome — and on whose terms.

name: OpenAI
title: The Ball in OpenAI's Court - Business Insider
description:
The White House declined to provide an on-the-record statement for this story, and connected me with a current official who asked to remain anonymous.
The current White House official contested this account, saying Ball had little impact on the AI Action Plan's policy process or wording.
Ball left that August, after less than five months at the White House, and before obtaining a security clearance.
The White House official shared this view, but added that given the administration's current stance on Ball, they're surprised OpenAI hired him.
This fits a prediction I heard from David Krueger, an AI safety researcher who thinks Ball doesn't take the idea of powerful superintelligence seriously enough.
text:
On a gloomy July evening, Dean Ball is appraising the political theory shelf in the basement of San Francisco's City Lights Bookstore. It's the end of his second day at OpenAI, and he's arrived straight from orientation in a cashmere zip-up hoodie, carrying a company-issued tote bag. He pulls a copy of Friedrich Hayek's "The Pure Theory of Capital" from the shelf, notes how rare it is to see it in the wild, and flips through its pages. It's a fitting choice.

Ball has landed in a distinctly Hayekian role at OpenAI. The 20th century economist, as Ball recounts to me, argued that political change begins not at the ballot box but among intellectuals, whose ideas would eventually filter into government. His work inspired a generation of right-wing think tanks that helped remake American politics. One of them, the Manhattan Institute, gave Ball his first job after college.

In June, OpenAI announced that it had hired the 34-year-old Ball to lead its new "strategic futures" team, a think tank of sorts, charged with shaping AI policy from within the company. It's a broad mandate for a nervy time. Nearly everyone agrees artificial intelligence is becoming more powerful; many believe it could become catastrophically dangerous. In late July a rogue OpenAI agent hacked into the AI startup Hugging Face's systems on its own, sending a fresh wave of fears about the technology's capacities. There is little agreement over how, when, or by whom AI should be regulated.

If Ball — who's made a name for himself as a voluble Substack writer and as a key author of the Trump administration's AI Action Plan — gets his way, the AI labs will become what he calls a "counterbalance to government." They will continue to churn out increasingly powerful technology, unconstrained by laws that would ban development or preempt upheaval in the labor market. "Dean has spent a lot of time thinking seriously about some of the biggest questions frontier AI labs need to get right," Ball's new boss, OpenAI strategy head Jason Kwon, said in a statement. "He'll help us pressure-test our assumptions," Kwon added, and think through questions around AI safety, economic impacts, and the "evolving relationship between governments, companies, and society." Ball tells me he wants to articulate genuinely new visions for what superintelligent AI can deliver. He'll leave direct lobbying to others. "I'm way too spiky of a guy for that," he says.

Spiky is right — Ball's rise from local policy wonk into AI's elite has earned him a fair share of enemies. Some critics say he's a naive AI booster, others that his AI-era William F. Buckley persona is a put-on. Emil Michael, who leads the Pentagon's research and engineering office, called Ball the "supreme village idiot" of AI in a July post to X, adding, "Dean Ball has perhaps the biggest gap between actual IQ and his own perceived IQ of anyone in the industry (about 40 points)." Michael isn't his only former colleague to disavow him. The White House declined to provide an on-the-record statement for this story, and connected me with a current official who asked to remain anonymous. The official tells me that Ball is no longer trusted by the administration and claims that he's dramatically inflated his impact on the action plan.

Ball says he still has friends in the administration and people across agencies that he advises every day. There are people he's pissed off, too, but the idea that he inflated his input on the action plan is "completely false," he says. "If you mean it, say it on the fucking record."

I spoke with Ball a few times during his first weeks at OpenAI. A self-described "information hedonist," he's equally delighted to dissect avant-garde film as influential policy research. Over a dinner in San Francisco, he pontificated about the Enlightenment, cited many of his own predictions, spoke in machine-learning analogies and Latin phrases, and said that parts of Biden-era AI policy were "woke shit." He's become an influential figure within AI's executive class, making him a useful weather vane for the technology's changing political winds.

Ball was raised middle-class in Northern Virginia, by parents with what he called "lib-coded" jobs. His dad, a punk rock drummer turned therapist, would take him on ride-alongs to clients struggling with substance abuse. "I saw a lot of shit when I was young. He exposed me to that stuff," he says. Finishing high school in 2010, Ball still felt "apathetic" about politics.

He arrived at Hamilton College, the upstate New York liberal arts school, to find that the professor he'd adored in a pre-enrollment lecture had been denied tenure and had left for the Alexander Hamilton Institute, a conservative think tank nearby. Ball visited, joined a Hayek reading group, and was bowled over. The idea that he wasn't being handed the economist's work in his regular college classes felt ludicrous.

"I kind of just realized, wait, fighting in the battle of ideas is totally what I want to be doing," Ball says. "Because this is ridiculous. This guy is so much smarter than any of my professors and the fact that my professors would deign to tell me I shouldn't read him for whatever stupid, narrow-minded reason they have, I cannot abide by that." He started inhaling right-of-center political theory.

After graduating, he joined the Manhattan Institute, focusing on city and state policy. Vanessa Mendoza, his boss at the time, says that when she met Ball, he stuck out as an "immediate adult." He would come early and stay late to hear from scholars outside his remit, and went on to work at think tanks for over a decade.

After ChatGPT's release at the end of 2022, Ball began to worry that conservatives weren't seriously considering how powerful AI could become. If a guy with a nanotechnology fabricator destroys the galaxy, he quips, Americans will probably lose some individual liberties. He eventually decided to enter the fray, launching his Substack, "Hyperdimensional," at the beginning of 2024. He began with a spritely free-market screed, declaring that he would write from a "classical liberal and un-apologetically pro-progress perspective." The private sector had "grown up"; its firms wielded capital that "would make Stalin and the rest of the 20th century's foremost central planners blush."

Ball writes in a high-minded first person. He deploys "fundamentally," "necessarily," and "profoundly" often for emphasis. He profoundly loves nautical metaphors. America's founding ideals are "our sole ballasts against the gusts"; a White House staffer's work requires cutting through the "hull of a gargantuan ship" in search of the engine room. AI policy, as of July 2024, was an oceanic abyss: "You can try to cast an anchor into the bottomless sea, but the ship will just start sinking, inch by inch."

In July, Emil Michael tweeted that "Dean Ball has perhaps the biggest gap between actual IQ and his own perceived IQ of anyone in the industry (about 40 points)."

He started making his name among AI's elite later that year, when he leaped into the fight over a proposed bill in California that would have created a board to regulate AI models and mandated safety protocols for AI labs. Even the safety-minded researchers whom he opposed were impressed with Ball's thoughtfulness, which stood out amid bad-faith takes from the anti-regulation side. He wasn't "caricaturing or being deceptive" but engaging with the actual text, Helen Toner, an OpenAI board member at the time, tells me. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said on a podcast that Ball's "scholarly" writing helped him understand the bill, which Gov. Gavin Newsom eventually vetoed.

Then Trump won the 2024 election. Ball didn't yet think he'd built the reputation to win a job, but suddenly heard from a member of the transition team.

During the first week of his new term, Trump signed an executive order on AI, calling for his administration to draft a pro-business policy that would "sustain and enhance America's global AI dominance in order to promote human flourishing, economic competitiveness, and national security."

Ball joined a team led by Michael Kratsios, Trump's policy director for science and technology, and David Sacks, his AI and crypto advisor, and the task soon took over his life. Ball says he "held the pen" on this policy document, writing the 20-plus-page first draft himself and, over the coming months, crafting several new versions with feedback from the leaders and the dozens of federal agencies that the plan's proposals would affect.

The current White House official contested this account, saying Ball had little impact on the AI Action Plan's policy process or wording. Kratsios and Sacks had sign-off on the plan, and dozens of staffers contributed, the official added. Ball says it's "just not accurate" that his role was minor.

The administration published the plan in July, with recommendations for countering Chinese influence and convening meetings about evaluating AI, amid dozens of other ideas. It was effectively a strategy document; none of it is binding, and many of the recommendations remain incomplete.

Ball left that August, after less than five months at the White House, and before obtaining a security clearance. He tells me the work was done: He'd joined to write the action plan, and then written it. He says he realized he'd be more effective as a writer and commentator from the outside — especially since he felt the administration was downplaying AI's progress.

He began a new phase as an AI talking head, as his audience continued to grow on X and Substack, and he was repeatedly quoted in the press as a "former White House official." In February, when the Department of Defense designated Anthropic as a national security supply chain risk over a contract dispute, Ball tore into his old employer. "Our public institutions behaved erratically, maliciously, and without strategic clarity," he wrote. "Our political leaders conveyed little understanding of their own actions, to say nothing of the technology and its stakes."

Another spat opened up between Anthropic and the administration in April, and Ball again criticized the government's response. Ball had gone to work inside the "belly of the beast," as Max Bodach, a friend of Ball's and former think tank colleague, tells me, but came out with his same, classic, libertarian distrust of the state. Bodach said he thinks Ball has won more and more respect because "he really prizes his independence of thought above everything else in life."

Anthropic's contentious relationship with the White House — Trump called its leaders "left-wing nut jobs" at one point — has given many in the AI world the impression that OpenAI is the cannier political player. The White House official shared this view, but added that given the administration's current stance on Ball, they're surprised OpenAI hired him.

Despite his distaste for state intervention, Ball does believe the time is right for some regulation — or, as he put it on X, "moderate prudence beyond what the incentives of advanced capitalism on its own might provide for." As AI models advance, an industry consensus is emerging on the need for mandatory safety testing. Anthropic's Amodei, Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis, and OpenAI have each recently suggested ideas for government-backed safety audits.

Ball has voiced support for versions of this idea for over a year — he particularly liked the AI nonprofit METR's recent holistic audit of the labs, in which the auditors collaborated with the industry while reckoning with the current dangers of the tech.

Over the coming months, Ball says, he hopes to build a stronger consensus on what the safety audit structure might actually look like. "We need a common communal sense of like what these auditors are going to do exactly," he says. "What is in scope? What is out of scope? What is the point of them?"

OpenAI's global affairs team, the group more directly responsible for lobbying, takes the lead on regulatory matters in DC and at state capitols. That team has drawn critics, in part due to its leader, Chris Lehane, who helped advise the pro-AI, anti-regulation super PAC Leading the Future.

Nathan Calvin, an AI policy researcher who opposed Ball in the California bill fight but has since come to see him as a friend, said he hopes Ball can act as a counterweight to the global affairs team. Ball, Calvin says, could be "someone who is trying to make sure that the policies that OpenAI is putting forward are of the moment, and taking things seriously."

Ball says his team's long-term remit will be reckoning with the evolving questions about superintelligent AI and the relationships between labs and government along the way. So far, the new hire has mostly given OpenAI unwelcome publicity. After the July release of a new open-weight model by the Chinese lab Moonshot AI, Ball published a 660-word X post, writing that a world where open-weight models — which allow anyone to download and tweak the tech — are dominant could end with "full AI communism." He also suggested the models deter frontier AI research spending, and that the Trump administration might realize their "best strategy here" would be to cloak Chinese models in regulatory risk.

When you work for an industry, people are more skeptical about what you're saying, and are more likely to ask, 'Is this person a shill?'David Krueger

A wave of vitriol followed, including the Pentagon staffer's "village idiot" comment and a barb from Sacks, as Ball's post soared past 10 million views. A narrative emerged that Ball was just talking his book as an OpenAI employee.

Before Ball took the OpenAI job, he'd secured a guarantee in his contract that he'd still be able to write independently on X and his Substack. ("TBPN," the chummy tech news streaming show OpenAI acquired in April, has similarly said that it remains editorially independent.) But the response was a bitter lesson.

"It is effectively impossible to do the kind of writing I used to do on this website, not because anyone at OpenAI censors me but because of the sheer volume of hostility I get for sharing my analysis as a frontier lab employee," Ball wrote on X.

This fits a prediction I heard from David Krueger, an AI safety researcher who thinks Ball doesn't take the idea of powerful superintelligence seriously enough. Krueger says that he hopes Ball's position at OpenAI will detract from his credibility. "When you work for an industry, people are more skeptical about what you're saying, and are more likely to ask, 'Is this person a shill?'" he says. "And I think that's healthy and good."

Alex Turner, an AI safety researcher who recently left Google DeepMind, says that while he's appreciated Ball's thoughtfulness in the past, "I feel like usually when people go to a lab, they become much less able to think clearly about what their group is doing, what their lab is doing. I'd hate to see that happen to Dean."

Ball tells me that his opinions haven't changed much since his start at OpenAI, and that if anything, he's more pro-regulatory. But he's realizing he's now seen differently. The first month on the job has been a tricky one for AI policy's most prominent critic — just as the stakes get higher and the politics get gnarlier.

"My job relies on me maintaining some degree of credibility, and ability to speak to a diverse array of people and not just a sort of predictable set of allies, right?" Ball told me a week before his open-source post. "That's the heart of what I do for a living. If I'm in a world where I can't do that, it's a real problem."

text:
OpenAI has acquired NextSlide, an artificial intelligence startup specializing in automated presentation creation, a move that signals the company's intention to push ChatGPT deeper into the visual communication and productivity market. The deal, which took place earlier this year but was only publicly confirmed on August 8, 2026, sees the NextSlide team absorbed into OpenAI's workforce to directly contribute to ChatGPT's development.

Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed. NextSlide founder Ahmed Beshry confirmed the acquisition in a statement on the company's website and in a LinkedIn post, noting that the announcement was coming "a few months late" given the deal had already closed. "We're joining OpenAI," Beshry wrote, adding that his team is now working on ChatGPT.

NextSlide developed a platform designed to transform user prompts, notes, documents, or research materials into polished, editable presentations. The core mission, according to Beshry, was "to make visual communication more accessible and help more people express their ideas clearly." By integrating with OpenAI, the team intends to "continue pursuing that same mission: building AI products that help people create, communicate, and turn their ideas into meaningful work."

Beshry is a serial entrepreneur with a track record of building AI-driven startups that attract major acquirers. He previously co-founded Caper AI, a company focused on smart shopping carts and cashier-less checkout technology. Instacart acquired Caper AI in 2021, providing a blueprint for a founder-led exit to a larger platform seeking to enhance its technological capabilities.

The acquisition is a clear indicator of OpenAI's ambition to evolve ChatGPT beyond a text-based conversational agent into a multimodal productivity suite. By embedding presentation-generation capabilities directly into ChatGPT, OpenAI could streamline workflows for millions of professionals who currently toggle between drafting text in a chatbot and designing slides in separate software. The integration is expected to allow users to generate not only the written content for a presentation but also its visual structure and design, all within a single interface. This positions ChatGPT to compete more directly with entrenched productivity tools, including Microsoft PowerPoint's AI-powered Designer and Copilot features, as well as specialized presentation platforms like Gamma and Tome.

For the broader AI industry, the deal underscores a trend where frontier model developers are acquiring small, specialized startups not necessarily for raw technology, but for talent and product vision. NextSlide's team brings a user-centric approach to visual communication, a domain where large language models have shown potential but often lack refined, user-friendly implementation. The acquisition could accelerate the rollout of features that bridge the gap between conversational AI and tangible business outputs, a critical battleground as enterprises demand more than just text generation from their AI subscriptions.

The move also raises questions about the competitive landscape. Microsoft, a major backer and infrastructure partner of OpenAI, operates PowerPoint as a core component of its Office 365 ecosystem. While the two companies maintain a complex, multi-layered partnership, the addition of native presentation features to ChatGPT creates an interesting overlap. It remains to be seen whether this will be positioned as a complementary tool or a more direct alternative to traditional software.

Investors and industry analysts will be watching closely for any signals on how OpenAI plans to monetize enhanced visual features. While the company has aggressively pursued enterprise clients with ChatGPT Team and ChatGPT Enterprise tiers, a robust presentation tool could justify higher subscription pricing or attract a new segment of business users who prioritize visual content creation. The lack of disclosed financial terms makes it difficult to gauge the deal's size, but the acquisition of an entire team suggests a strategic commitment rather than a minor acqui-hire.

Beshry's experience at Caper AI also hints at a potential long-term play in retail and visual interfaces. While there is no indication that OpenAI plans to enter the smart cart space, the combination of computer vision expertise and language models could eventually lead to novel applications in physical retail environments or augmented reality presentations.

As the NextSlide team settles into OpenAI, users can expect a phased integration of presentation capabilities into ChatGPT, likely starting with basic slide generation from prompts and expanding to more sophisticated design controls. The acquisition reinforces the message that the AI arms race is increasingly about owning the entire user workflow, from idea to finished product, rather than just providing the underlying model.

title: Grayson Brulte: Uber's Robotaxi Strategy Faces a Permit Problem, Not a Technology Problem
description:

text:
Uber's Q2 earnings were fine. Bookings beat expectations. The stock still sold off into the low $60s, and the bulls on X scrambled to offer the equivalent of "Pedialyte and Gatorade to get over the hangover," as Grayson Brulte put it. The problem is structural, not quarterly: Uber finally acknowledged the $10 billion Financial Times number for its autonomous-vehicle commitment, and the market is doing the uncomfortable math. That money — a mix of equity investments in AV companies that will need more capital and contractual commitments to purchase vehicles that aren't being built at scale yet — has to solve for 100,000 robotaxis on the network by 2028–2030. On the Road to Autonomy podcast, Brulte and Walter Piecyk of LightShed Research spent 48 minutes on a single question: now that the money is real and the permits are landing, who actually controls the rider — the AV operator, the aggregator, or the regulator?

The $10 billion commitment and the distribution-moat illusion

Uber's autonomy thesis rests on a simple argument: AV companies will need Uber's network because building dispatch infrastructure is hard. Dara Khosrowshahi said on the earnings call that the Waymo relationship continues next year contractually, and Uber projects expansion from seven cities today to 28 globally by end of 2028.

Brulte's counter-argument is that the assumption is already breaking. "At some point, the brand will get stronger, some of these AV companies than Uber, and they'll realize that they don't need Uber because it's not hard to build an app," he said. The Zoox launch in Las Vegas is the exhibit: Aicha Evans has painted Harry Reid International Airport green with "download the app" advertising, and Khosrowshahi now concedes Zoox will live on both the Uber app and its own app. Waymo, meanwhile, is preparing a standalone Austin service once the Uber exclusivity expires in 2028 — a move confirmed by a Waymo spokesperson this week that signals deepening tensions between the two companies.

Piecyk unpacked the $10 billion number as less transformative than the headline implies. The car purchases "will take time," he noted. "They're not buying thousands of cars soon." Brulte was more direct: $10 billion is insufficient for the stated goal, and the market structure will shift before the fleet materializes. The information flow for Uber stock over the next 12 months is not friendly — Waymo will simply extend its lead in cars on the road — even if the fortunes turn at the promised scale in 2028–2030.

Las Vegas: Zoox gets paid, and the 45 mph ceiling bites

Zoox launches paid rides on August 10, 2026 — the first commercial service using a vehicle purpose-built without steering wheels or pedals, a milestone secured by a July 31 NHTSA exemption from eight Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards. The public narrative is triumphant. The underlying data is thinner.

Rob at OMEGA, Brulte's research partner, pulled the public NHTSA filing: Zoox vehicles are restricted from operating above 45 mph. AAA data cited in the episode puts average traffic speed leaving Las Vegas Airport at 55 mph, with access roads at 45 to 60 mph. Driving below the flow of traffic, Brulte argued, is itself a safety hazard — and the airport is the trip that anchors the premium-use case. The fleet count is 105 Zooxmobiles as of June 2026, spread across seven approved cities, five named in NHTSA filings and two redacted. A friend of the show tried to hail a Zoox in Vegas the day before recording and got "service unavailable"; Brulte corrected Piecyk that the quoted wait was 75 minutes, not 15.

Pricing is positioned at 20 to 40 percent above average rideshare, represented on the Uber app at the Comfort tier with a base fare plus time and distance and no reroute penalty. Brulte's verdict: "This is not luxury pricing, it is tourism pricing." When a premium product lets you neither choose your destination nor get a car quickly, pricing power evaporates.

The competitive context in Vegas is about to get crowded, and Waymo's freeway return matters beyond the Strip. After a two-month pause tied to construction zones, Waymo can again take highways, which Piecyk called "the airport unlock." Brulte reinforced it with the SFO example — the airport route to the Peninsula or the city requires the highway, and surface-street punishment rides are a reason riders defect.

The Lucid-Nuro-Uber countdown: California blocks the door, Texas holds it open

Lucid's Q2 report was brutal — the stock got crushed, gross margin came in at roughly negative 100 percent, the company burned over $1 billion in the quarter, and deliveries reached just 4,000 units. The offset: Lucid has formally designated autonomy its top strategic priority, placed the Uber-Nuro robotaxi work inside a new "Lucid Technologies" entity, and called the project a "must-win." Piecyk remained wary that the structure shields the robotaxi business inside a protected entity while the rest of the company struggles. The scale contrast is stark: 4,000 quarterly deliveries against a 35,000-unit Nuro program target.

Can the trio deliver a paid robotaxi launch in California by year-end? Brulte's answer is a flat no. His conviction stems from two decades of observing state regulators: "Your first launch market for a robotaxi service should never be California." The permit path allows unpaid testing — Brulte gave "high likelihood and high probability" of a free-service launch by year-end — but the paid-service approvals will not clear in time. For Uber, that matters: Piecyk noted the company only counts a market as launched when payment is enabled on its app.

The escape hatch is Texas. If California blocks the paid launch, Brulte posited an Uber-Nuro launch in Houston by year-end, where the regulatory path is clear. A 25-to-30-car paid launch anywhere, even with safety drivers, would read as a win for all three companies. "If you can get something launched in any market — 25, 30 cars, ideally with not a driver in there — by the end of the year," Piecyk said, "get something on the tape, and then you kind of move forward."

ScenarioConditionsExpected market reactionPaid SF launch, year-end 2026Regulatory approvals clear; unlikely per host analysisPositive but priced-in; Waymo scale gap remainsFree-only California servicePermits allow testing, not revenueMixed — "you put all this money in and you can't charge?"Houston pivotRegulatory environment forces relocationVery positive for Uber, Lucid, Nuro — tangible launch

Brulte closed the arc with an open question: at some point, does Lucid simply become a contract manufacturer for robotaxis and shut down the sedan and Gravity consumer business? "If Lucid can figure out the business, figure out the manufacturing, and hit the manufacturing targets, Uber has a very clear line of sight to vehicles," he said. "That's one of the most difficult things that happens in this industry." The question of whether Lucid's consumer business survives that transformation is the investment-relevant variable to track alongside the production ramp.

NVIDIA's open model, and the Level 4 system nobody runs

On August 4, 2026, Jensen Huang released Alpamayo 2 Super, NVIDIA's open autonomy model, which has already seen 500,000 downloads on Hugging Face. The Mercedes partnership reveals the architecture: NVIDIA's open model plus its full stack, with an arbiter layer that sits between the two — the traditional stack proposes one trajectory, the open model proposes another, and the system decides. Piecyk's point is that this dual-trajectory arbitration is what Uber should want more OEMs to adopt.

Brulte reads the open-model release through a CUDA lens — the strategic goal is locking companies into the NVIDIA developer ecosystem early, because "once you build on that platform, it's very hard then to go swap into a TI, to a Qualcomm." Piecyk is skeptical the lock-in works for the OEMs that matter: GM and Ford would still have to build their own full stack, and he doubts the cultural DNA exists.

Then Brulte set the milestone the industry should demand: "To my knowledge, there is not a SAE Level 4 robotaxi operating anywhere in the world that is full stack NVIDIA." The distinction between supervised and unsupervised miles, he said, is "completely different," and until an NVIDIA full-stack car runs driverless at real scale, the OEM pitch remains theoretical. The Mercedes timeline is the test: rides on Uber with safety drivers in the first half of 2027, driver-out likely 2028.

The sleeper in the stack war is Qualcomm: the Snapdragon Digital Chassis developer documentation is, per Brulte, genuinely impressive, Qualcomm holds a healthy L2/L2+ business, it already has the BMW deal, and it is positioned to "knock out a big chunk of Mobileye business" before eventually licensing an L4 system. NVIDIA as service provider and critical infrastructure player, yes; NVIDIA as deployed full-stack competitor, unproven.

London's APS permit will decide who owns the passenger

The most consequential regulatory document of the summer is not in California or Texas. It is London's Automated Passenger Service permit — a five-year license, renewable six months before expiry, that "controls who controls the service," in Brulte's formulation. Wayve's new Transport for London for-hire license lets it carry paying passengers with a safety or test driver; reported permits cover 15 vehicles. But the APS permit is the strategic layer: any holder can launch a service without an aggregator.

Brulte's predictions, developed in detail in the OMEGA research service and The Road to Autonomy newsletter, were delivered on the podcast with unusual clarity. Waymo gets the APS permit and operates fully on its own, own app and fleet. Wayve wants to be a pure licensing company — its marketing explicitly says so — so expect Uber to hold the permit while Wayve licenses the stack. Then there is Baidu: FreeNow currently holds the operating license, not Lyft, but if Baidu secures the APS, it can exit the FreeNow relationship entirely and launch Apollo Go in London directly.

"Watch the market for who owns the APS permit," Brulte said. "The APS permit, in my opinion, is an asset 'cause that controls who controls the service." If Uber loses that layer in London, the hangover travels.

Trucking: Pony.ai's numbers are missing a critical detail

Pony.ai formally put numbers on its robotruck ambitions this week: 500 to 1,000 Generation-4 trucks in two to three years, with CATL as partner, operating in mainland China — with a "foreign ports" clause Brulte speculates points to Rotterdam. The problem, he said, is what is not disclosed: "We don't have miles. We don't know whether supervised or unsupervised, and that's very important in autonomous trucking."

Piecyk's ranking was blunt: Aurora and Kodiak are ahead of that curve. Aurora was reportedly cited in a Teamsters lawsuit filed in Alameda Superior Court seeking to repeal California's newly proposed autonomous-trucking regulations around its thousand-mile driverless run. Brulte's reaction was volcanic — "California's closed for business" — and he noted that if Attorney General Becerra wins the November 2026 gubernatorial election, the DMV rules get reversed anyway. Piecyk flagged a counter: a House bill in the pipeline would preempt state AV restrictions under the Commerce Clause, though he expects years of litigation either way.

Then came the contrarian call. "I say this for the record, I think Tesla Semi is a sleeper," Brulte said. Fleet operators who have tested the vehicle — names like Covenant Logistics' Matt McClellan and David Moss — reported it "worked great." The host trio wants a Reno factory visit, and Brulte's conviction is backed by on-the-ground operator feedback rather than chart analysis.

PlayerCurrent claimTargetOpen questionAuroraCited in Teamsters complaint re: thousand-mile driverless run; Texas-focusedDriver-out at scaleCalifornia regulatory reversal riskKodiakTexas-focused operationsAhead of Pony's paceReporting tonight, Aug 8Pony.ai500-1,000 Gen-4 trucks in 2-3 years, CATL partner, mainland ChinaForeign-port expansion (Rotterdam?)No miles, no supervision data disclosedTesla SemiTested by fleet operators — "worked great"Reno production rampBrulte calls it a sleeper

Delivery is the quiet autonomy market, and DoorDash is underselling it

DoorDash reported this week, and its analyst call exposed a strange gap: a company that invested in autonomy last year and saw its stock challenged by that investment now seems to be selling the autonomy upside short. Piecyk was struck by "the lack of optimism or potential that I saw for autonomy for food."

The hosts disagreed with the market's skepticism on substance. Delivery autonomy is a realistic market within five years, for reasons beyond the obvious. Rob at OMEGA flagged that the delivery use-case reduces deadhead miles, which cuts in your favor with local regulators — an underappreciated dimension of the economics. Brulte pointed to consumer fatigue: "America has tipping fatigue," and fee fatigue is real, which creates room for cost-efficient autonomous fulfillment.

The structural asymmetry matters more. In moving people, Waymo, Tesla, or Zoox can cut the aggregator out entirely because building an app is easy. In delivery, DoorDash and Uber hold the restaurant and retailer relationships, which is why autonomy is more likely to be an accelerant than an existential threat for them. Brulte's caveat: if a rider's own Tesla gets dispatched to Whole Foods and returns with groceries, that is a win for Amazon, not the aggregator. The bigger long-run risk is large restaurant chains refusing aggregator fees once autonomous fulfillment exists. "Do not discount big box retail," he said.

The cross-theme synthesis is that every headline this week traces to the same friction: deployment is regulated and physical before it is digital. One hundred five Zooxmobiles, 15 Wayve permits, a 45 mph NHTSA cap, 4,000 Lucid deliveries against a 35,000-unit ambition, a two-month Waymo freeway pause — the bottlenecks are vehicles, permits, and politics. Whoever resolves those three fastest decides who owns the rider. Brulte's closing line carries the thesis: "Autonomy is becoming an economy. The future is bright. The future is autonomous. The future is unsupervised." For investors, the question is who gets to charge for it.

In this episode of Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing, Motley Fool contributors Tyler Crowe, Matt Frankel, and Lou Whiteman discuss:

Meta and Microsoft’s earnings reports.

The best “Magnificent Seven” stock to buy now.

Hidden Gems earning highlights.

Maibag: Buy single stocks or bet on several companies in the same industry?
