name: OpenAI
title: OpenAI agents passed secret notes for months leading up to Hugging Face hack - Fortune
description:
Hugging Face disclosed the breach on July 16, followed by OpenAI claiming responsibility on July 21, which Fortune was first to report.
This is what would lead them to hack Hugging Face a few days later on July 9.
They first hacked into OpenAI’s infrastructure, though apparently didn’t find what they needed, so they went to Hugging Face.
It was only then that they able to connect the internal breach with the Hugging Face breach later in July, tracing them both back to the same internal testing.
Agents often negotiate, share information, delegate tasks, and adapt to each others’ actions, according to an Amazon article on AI agents.
text:
On stage at the Black Hat cybersecurity conference in Las Vegas, OpenAI alignment and safety researcher Eric Wallace along with infrastructure and security engineer Michael Dalton explained that the origins of the breach go back to May 7 when OpenAI was internally testing an unreleased model, according to a report from Ground Level AI, which attended the session.

That’s over two months before the rogue agents entered Hugging Face’s servers on July 9. Hugging Face disclosed the breach on July 16, followed by OpenAI claiming responsibility on July 21, which Fortune was first to report.

In Las Vegas, the OpenAI execs explained for the first time that as part of training back in May, the company’s researchers prompted the AIs with tasks that should have been impossible under the constraints of the testing environment.

In order to tackle the challenge, the OpenAI execs explained, the model spun out multiple iterations of itself, or agents. The agents then began to work together, leaving messages for each other on an internal messaging board. They did this by saving files of notes for one another in a repository. That way, if an agent discovered a system vulnerability, or got access to a server it wasn’t supposed to, it could leave a note for the others to let them know about it.

This sequence of events reveals how the agents appeared to decide on their own that working collaboratively, rather than individually, would get them to their goal faster.

OpenAI discovered its models’ messages and shut down the operation in early July. The company apparently had its own internal security incident on July 4, after which it revoked the ability for agents to post messages. (Perhaps we will learn more about that incident when OpenAI releases its post-mortem.)

But, as the executives explained on Wednesday, OpenAI’s attempt to curtail the agents’ messaging abilities was not entirely successful. Instead, the agents proved to be persistent, and spun up a new version of a messaging board—with a twist. Rather than leaving messages in files, they created directories, and used their new names as messages. This is what would lead them to hack Hugging Face a few days later on July 9.

In the messages, the agents discussed that they needed more information to complete their impossible tasks, and reasoned that the material might live on an external website such as GitHub or Hugging Face. They first hacked into OpenAI’s infrastructure, though apparently didn’t find what they needed, so they went to Hugging Face. In OpenAI’s internal post-mortem, a public version of which it says it will release in the coming weeks, it was able to connect these two breaches.

Agent collaboration is a feature, not a bug

It appears OpenAI did not know the agents hacked an outside company until Hugging Face disclosed the incident. It was only then that they able to connect the internal breach with the Hugging Face breach later in July, tracing them both back to the same internal testing.

Agent collaboration is actually a trend in the AI industry, Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue tells Fortune. For that reason, he was “not so surprised” to hear of OpenAI’s agents colluding. Hugging Face hosts spaces for agents to collaborate. In one example on the site, humans can click an “Add Your Agent” button to launch their AIs into the fray. They coordinate activities through a shared messaging board.

Another example of agents collaborating can be found in the Elon Musk-owned xAI , which recently added four agents to its Grok 4.2 model, naming them Grok, Harper, Benjamin, and Lucas. They “debate internally [and] fact-check each other in real time,” writes one user. Agents often negotiate, share information, delegate tasks, and adapt to each others’ actions, according to an Amazon article on AI agents. Each completes its portion of the project, and then reports back to the group.

“For example, multi-agent systems in healthcare can have agents specializing in specific tasks like diagnosis, preventive care, medicine scheduling, etc., for holistic patient care automation,” Amazon says.

The problem going forward is how to make sure the agents are not working toward a nefarious goal, or that they do not commit crimes, such as hacking, to achieve their desired outcome. Responsibility for any liability that arises from rogue agents like the ones that attacked Hugging Face could likely fall on the AI company that created the agents designed its prompts, and what internal controls it puts in place.

Companies like OpenAI could “analyze the agent logs and traces” to see what they’ve been doing, Delangue said, adding that “[he’s] not really sure why frontier labs don’t do this to be honest, that sounds like 101 of agent monitoring, especially at the frontier.” He personally asked OpenAI to release the redacted agent traces after the hack.

Meanwhile, regulators have been slow to develop regimes to carry out oversight in how AI companies operate. The Trump administration met this week with the leading AI labs in Washington D.C. to discuss a safety framework for powerful new model releases.

The framework calls for companies to submit their models to the government for review 30 days prior to their debut. However, the administration has decided not to publicize the framework, or any details, such as the companies that will participate, or the criteria for which models are eligible, leaving the public and rest of the AI industry in the dark.

In disclosing the details of the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI did not share this new information in a blog post or written report, as is typical with security incidents. Instead, it elected to provide the details at the Black Hat conference in Las Vegas after organizers reached out to OpenAI and asked the company to speak.

text:
By Christine Ji

Trade Desk's revenue growth slowed to just 3% in the second quarter

A drawn-out fee dispute with advertising agency Publicis Groupe weighed on Trade Desk's sales this year.

Trade Desk's growth struggles deepened in the second quarter, as the company posted an earnings and revenue miss combined with disappointing guidance.

Shares of Trade Desk (TTD) fell 23% in after-market trading Thursday following the results, deepening a year-long slide for the stock. The digital-advertising company has been facing macro headwinds as closed online ecosystems seize greater portions of advertising budgets, resulting in slowing top-line growth.

The company posted revenue of $715 million for the June quarter, falling short of the $752 million anticipated by analysts polled by FactSet and growing a mere 3% year over year. Revenue growth at Trade Desk has slowed significantly in recent quarters: The same time a year ago, the company posted 19% growth year over year. Adjusted earnings of 34 cents per share also missed consensus analyst expectations of 40 cents.

"This quarter did not meet the standard we set for ourselves, but it has reinforced our belief that we are focused on the right opportunities for the future," CEO Jeff Green shared in a press release.

"While there is work ahead, I am confident our actions will help marketers drive better business outcomes and support the shift of media budgets toward the open internet," he added.

Down 53% this year so far, Trade Desk is the second-worst performing stock in the S&P 500 SPX in 2026. The company's forward earnings multiple has compressed to 16, down from the nearly 90 multiple it commanded just a year ago, according to FactSet.

Trade Desk's third-quarter guidance also disappointed investors. Management forecasted revenue of $650 million, missing Wall Street estimates of $807 million. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization are expected to be approximately $160 million.

On the earnings call, Green shared that most of the company's revenue comes from Fortune 500 companies. "All of our customers are operating in a fundamentally different environment than they were even a year ago," he said. Consumer packaged goods and auto companies are "overrepresented" on the platform, making up 25% of the business, and those companies have been hit hard by tariffs and oil prices, Green added.

Artificial intelligence is also changing the nature of the advertising industry, which Green believes will lead to more competition.

The company's drawn-out dispute with advertising agent Publicis Groupe (PUBGY) has also hurt revenue and weighed on the stock. In March, a third-party audit commissioned by Publicis accused Trade Desk of levying hidden fees, leading the agency to remove Trade Desk from its recommended platform list and urge clients to pause spending.

The two companies reached an agreement in June, but it's unclear when or if revenue will return to predispute levels, Benchmark analyst Mark Zgutowicz wrote in a Thursday note.

-Christine Ji

name: Microsoft
title: Microsoft is bringing AI to Windows 11's performance tools to figure out why PCs are slow ...
description:
Windows already has performance tools that the company’s engineers, third-party developers, and OEM partners use to determine why PCs are slow or acting up.
Right now, you can’t easily connect AI to Windows performance tools and ask questions such as, “Why was this PC slow?” You need to manually search through data, including tables, processes, call stacks, and more.
Microsoft says it’s testing AI integration in Windows Performance Analyzer (WPA).
MCP stands for Model Context Protocol, and it allows AI to connect to tools such as Windows Performance Analyzer.
In this case, GitHub Copilot can communicate with Windows Performance Analyzer and answer your questions.
text:
Microsoft’s leadership, including CEO Satya Nadella, has admitted that Windows 11 needs serious “quality work,” and we’re already seeing some progress, but most of the changes have focused on UI/UX. We’ve been told a faster Windows is coming, but how does the company plan to figure out why a PC is running slowly? AI-powered diagnosis.

Windows already has performance tools that the company’s engineers, third-party developers, and OEM partners use to determine why PCs are slow or acting up.

Right now, you can’t easily connect AI to Windows performance tools and ask questions such as, “Why was this PC slow?” You need to manually search through data, including tables, processes, call stacks, and more.

Microsoft says it’s testing AI integration in Windows Performance Analyzer (WPA). The company argues that WPA is one of the most important tools for analyzing performance issues on a PC, and it’s used by developers who work directly on Windows, as well as partners such as Intel and AMD.

The company has built a new MCP for Windows Performance Analyzer, so its developers or anyone else can use an AI tool such as GitHub Copilot to ask why the CPU spiked, what’s using the disk, or why scheduling is acting up. There are many other areas of Windows that you can monitor or benchmark using WPA, and all of them are getting AI integration.

What is MCP, and how is it going to help Microsoft and its partners make Windows faster?

MCP stands for Model Context Protocol, and it allows AI to connect to tools such as Windows Performance Analyzer. In a way, it’s similar to add-ins for Excel, but it’s far more powerful. In this case, GitHub Copilot can communicate with Windows Performance Analyzer and answer your questions.

Of course, it’s not meant for regular users because you cannot necessarily fix Windows issues just by asking AI what caused them. It’s intended for Windows developers, including those who work at Microsoft, Intel, and other partners.

Nobody should be surprised that Microsoft is using AI to optimize Windows, and it’s not exactly a bad idea because the integration is actually quite useful.

When you turn on WPA MCP, you can use GitHub Copilot CLI inside the WPA trace-analysis workflow. You don’t have to dig through graphs and tables to determine what caused the problem because AI does the heavy lifting, and you can ask questions in natural language. You can also use AI to generate a summary of its findings.

For example, developers can open Windows Performance Analyzer and ask whether a slowdown was caused by CPU starvation, disk activity, memory pressure, paging, or a driver.

“Performance analysis is often bottlenecked by expert knowledge. Experienced WPA users can move quickly, but new or occasional users may not know where to begin,” Microsoft noted in a document. “Even experts can spend significant time correlating activity across views before they reach a useful conclusion.”

Microsoft has been using WPA’s AI tools internally to investigate Windows performance concerns, and it makes sense to bring it to everyone.

The integration can also help anyone who develops apps, drivers, or hardware for the operating system identify input delays, regressions, CPU activity, memory activity, scheduling issues, and other problems using natural-language questions.

However, Microsoft warns that WPA MCP is an early preview, and it’s not a finished product, so it supports only GitHub Copilot and requires an active subscription. One more thing about the feature is that it can make mistakes, and findings can be incomplete or incorrect, so developers still need to verify everything at the end of the day.

Windows 11 is testing 8GB RAM optimization

In addition to an AI-powered performance analyzer, Microsoft is optimizing RAM usage for Windows 11 and its apps, including apps built using WinUI. There’s no denying that RAM prices have soared, and companies that control the supply chain have warned that prices are not going to come down anytime soon.

In fact, there are concerns that they could get worse in the coming months and become the new normal. Microsoft doesn’t control the supply chain, but it believes it can optimize Windows 11 for better performance on PCs with 8GB of RAM.

Microsoft says it’s working on scheduling and memory optimization improvements to help Windows run faster on PCs with 8GB of RAM. These changes will roll out over the coming months rather than as a single “performance boost drop.”

In 2025, Rivian's vehicle deliveries fell 18% year over year to 42,247 as it grappled with macro, supply chain, and competitive headwinds. name: Eli Lilly
title: Lilly built pharma's biggest AI supercomputer. Its Q2 numbers still do not show what AI is worth.
description:
Eli Lilly and Company is the company this series was built to test.
I read the Q2 2026 results to see whether it had.
[2] Eli Lilly and Company, Q2 2026 results press release, "Second-Quarter Reported Results," "Selected Revenue Highlights" and "2026 Financial Guidance" sections, 5 August 2026.
[4] Eli Lilly and Company, Q2 2026 earnings presentation, 55 slides, 5 August 2026.
[5] Eli Lilly and Company, Q2 2026 financial workbook (income statement, revenue, revenue growth, PRV, OID tabs), 5 August 2026.
text:
I am reading the H1 2026 results of the twenty largest pharmaceutical companies for one thing: whether the technology all of them say they run on has reached the part of the business that gets reported to investors. Two decades of my working life have gone into data, software and AI for drug R&D, and I want this to work, which is the bias to read everything below through. It is also why I use financial disclosure as the test. Companies are careful about what they put in front of the financial community, so it is the least forgiving place to look. My conclusion so far is that 2026 is the year the pace changed and that the returns have not arrived in the headline numbers yet. What sits one layer down is more interesting.

Eli Lilly and Company is the company this series was built to test. Among large drugmakers it is one of the loudest about technology and one of the most visible spenders on it: a wholly owned supercomputer, a billion-dollar lab with NVIDIA , an AI/ML platform opened to biotech (#TuneLab), a first-of-its-kind Chief AI Officer. If the returns from all of that are going to show up anywhere in the financial statements of a big pharma in 2026, Lilly is a reasonable place to look for them first. A company that promotes AI this heavily should, in principle, be among the first to report it. I read the Q2 2026 results to see whether it had.

What they told investors

Lilly reported worldwide revenue of $23.0 billion for the second quarter, up 48% as reported and 46% at constant exchange rates, with H1 revenue of $42.8 billion, up 51% [1]. Reported EPS was $7.94, up 26%; non-GAAP EPS was $8.38, up 33% [1]. Both figures carried $3.03 of acquired in-process R&D charges, against $0.14 a year earlier [1]. The engine was the incretin franchise: Mounjaro (tirzepatide; a once-weekly injectable GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist for type 2 diabetes) rose 91% to $9.9 billion and Zepbound (the same molecule, tirzepatide, branded for obesity and weight management) 46% to $4.9 billion, with Key Products revenue of $15.7 billion up 76%, and Key Products in immunology, oncology and neuroscience up 121% off a small base [1][2]. Growth was volume, not price. Volume added 60 points and realized price took 13 off, the pattern of a company trading price for access as it floods supply into the market [1][2].

The drag is in two places. The 13% price decline is the visible one, driven by Zepbound and Mounjaro and by the addition of Mounjaro to China's reimbursement list [2]. The other is the $2.8 billion acquired-IPR&D charge from the Orna and Ajax acquisitions, which cut reported profit and pushed the effective tax rate to 23.3%, because those charges are not deductible [2]. Lilly raised full-year revenue guidance to $85 to $87 billion and lifted underlying EPS by $2.78 at the midpoint, then handed most of that back: the same $3.03 of IPR&D charges left the EPS range at $35.50 to $36.50, slightly below the prior top end [1][2]. Lilly shares had fallen about 4.5% in the week before the release, and with expectations already high, analysts were focused on the size of the guidance raise rather than the quarter itself [3].

Now the two measurements I take from every release, both measures of disclosure prominence rather than of value, but comparable across all twenty companies. AI mentions in the results announcement, counted as a driver of anything: zero. The single instance of "artificial intelligence" in the press release sits in the forward-looking risk factors, in a sentence warning that the use of AI "may exacerbate" competitive, regulatory and cybersecurity risks [1]. The 55-slide results presentation does not credit AI, machine learning or digital with any reported line [4]. Does AI carry a number anywhere in the financials? No. I searched the full financial workbook: there is no technology, AI or digital line item in it [5].

The standard objection applies, and I will make it before someone else does. Earnings releases do not itemise the ERP system or the procurement platform, so AI's absence is not proof it created no value. That objection is weaker for Lilly than for anyone else in this series, because Lilly has already said, in public and on the record, that AI created value large enough to matter to these exact statements. Which brings me to the part of the record most people writing about Lilly's AI have not connected to the filing.

What they have already shown

Start with the thing that separates Lilly from every other company I have covered. In March 2026, Lilly's Chief Information and Digital Officer, Diogo Rau , told Forbes that AI let the company make more of its GLP-1 drugs than it otherwise could have. His words:

"We literally made more product last year than we possibly could have without AI," [and it was] "enough that it would've been material in our earnings reports" [6].

"Material" here is a CDO's colloquial "big enough to matter". The claim is also a counterfactual, that output was higher than it would have been without AI, and Rau does not disclose the baseline it is measured against. The mechanism is a manufacturing digital twin, a real-time virtual model of a factory that let Lilly simulate configurations of a production process it already believed was optimised, find a better one, and implement it. Rau's own description of the validation is the interesting part: "We thought, this looks too good to be true, but the physical world still matched the digital twin" [6]. A separate account from Lilly's manufacturing information lead describes the same approach resolving an identified process bottleneck, with a large reduction in the time that step took once the twin's prediction was piloted and rolled out [7].

The context is what makes it matter. During a period when Mounjaro and Zepbound demand outran supply, when the FDA had the drugs on shortage and compounders were legally copying them, additional output converted directly into revenue [6]. A named executive attributes some of that additional output to an AI system, and reports that the model's predictions matched physical production. On the evidence ladder I use across this series, that is a named production system with an operational effect, which is rung three, the rung where most credible companies sit. Among the companies assessed in this series, it is one of the strongest publicly described operational AI cases, alongside Sanofi 's, and it is different in kind from AstraZeneca 's clinical validation. What it is not, on the public record, is a quantified return.

The rest of the public record is unusually deep. Lilly TuneLab, launched in September 2025, opened 18 of Lilly's own drug-discovery AI/ML models to biotech partners, trained on datasets the company values at over $1 billion, using federated learning so partners run the models on their own data without exposing it [8]. LillyPod, announced in October 2025 and online by early 2026, is a wholly owned supercomputer built on 1,016 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs delivering more than 9,000 petaflops, which Lilly describes as the most powerful owned and operated by a pharmaceutical company [9] (that was before the recent Bristol Myers Squibb announcement). In January 2026 Lilly and NVIDIA committed up to $1 billion over five years to a co-innovation lab in South San Francisco, to build biology and chemistry foundation models and push toward automated, scientist-in-the-loop labs [10]. Underneath sits a run of business development aimed at the same capability, including an Insilico collaboration worth up to $2.75 billion and a model-building deal with Chai Discovery [6][11].

Two of those four are the manufacturing win and the drug-discovery bet, and they are at very different stages. The manufacturing twin has already happened and, by the CDO's account, already paid. The discovery infrastructure is a wager on the next decade, and Rau says so plainly: any medicine that comes from it arrives in the "mid-2030s, if not late-2030s," and he warns that expecting drugs in six or eighteen months is the overhyped claim most likely to discredit AI in the industry [6].

What they are building now

Lilly's AI leadership is senior and permanent. Thomas Fuchs became the company's first Chief AI Officer in October 2024, hired from Mount Sinai where he chaired AI and human health, with a mandate spanning discovery, clinical trials, manufacturing, commercial and internal functions [12]. He reports to Rau, the CIDO, who sits on Lilly's Executive Committee and reports to the CEO [12][13]. Technology has a seat at the top table and a named owner one level below it, which is the same structural pattern I found at Sanofi, where the Chief Digital Officer is a permanent Executive Committee member. In both companies AI has real internal authority. In both companies the earnings release records none of it.

Nothing in the Q2 release, the presentation or the guidance attributes any part of the 48% growth, the improved cost of production, or the manufacturing ramp to the digital twin Rau described to a magazine five months earlier [1][4][6]. The release credits the gross-margin improvement to "improved cost of production and favorable product mix" and stops there [1]. Dave Ricks opened the results saying Lilly is "building for the future," and named retatrutide (an investigational once-weekly GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist for obesity, Lilly's next-generation weight-loss candidate), new manufacturing capacity and business development as the pillars of that future [1]. He did not name the supercomputer he helped inaugurate ten months earlier, or the AI system his own CDO says was material to the company's ability to supply the drugs driving the quarter. The technology story and the earnings story are told by the same company to different audiences, and they do not reference each other.

The gap in this series is usually between capability and proof. At Lilly the capability is real and an operational effect is described on the record; what the filings withhold is the quantification. The distance is the last step, from "material, per the CDO, to a magazine" to a figure an investor could check in the results. Whether that step is missing because the effect cannot yet be isolated, because it does not meet Lilly's disclosure threshold, because it is commercially sensitive, or because Lilly does not treat it as a distinct financial driver, I cannot tell from outside, and the article that claimed to know would be overreaching.

Where that puts them

On the evidence ladder, Lilly sits at rung three, named production systems with operational metrics, the rung where most credible companies land, and the same rung as Sanofi , Roche and Novartis in this series. TuneLab, LillyPod and the discovery models are named, deployed and, in TuneLab's case, reaching external workflows, which clears the lower rungs comfortably. The manufacturing digital twin, a named system with an executive-attested operational effect and a report that the model matched physical production, is the strongest artefact holding the placement. What keeps it at three rather than higher is disclosure, not the work: the effect is unquantified, the baseline is undisclosed, and the account lives in a magazine rather than a filing. Rung four, model judgement checked against outcomes in a way an outsider can audit, and rung five, a model's prospective judgement written into a decision in advance and then tested, are where AstraZeneca sits in this series and almost no one else does.

What would move Lilly up is unusually concrete here, because the company has already done the hard part. A single disclosed sentence would do it: the manufacturing digital-twin effect reconciled into the cost-of-sales or volume commentary against a stated baseline and period, in the results rather than in an interview. That is a smaller step for Lilly than for any company I have covered, which is exactly why the silence is more striking.

What this does and does not prove

None of this shows AI drove Lilly's quarter. It did not, on the disclosure. The quarter was Mounjaro and Zepbound volume, a deliberate price-for-access trade, and an IPR&D charge, and Lilly says so [1][2]. Nor does the manufacturing story prove the discovery bet will pay: those are different problems on different timelines, and Rau himself puts any AI-originated medicine in the mid-to-late 2030s [6]. What the record does show is narrower. Lilly has a named, executive-attested operational AI effect in manufacturing, and its investor disclosures do not let a shareholder size it, isolate it from the parallel effect of billions in new capacity, or judge whether it recurs. That is a defensible position for a company to hold, on measurement grounds. It also means that among the industry's most visible investors in owned AI infrastructure, the one with the most public operational evidence has given the financial community, in its largest quarter, nothing it can measure the technology by.

What to watch

Lilly reports Q3 in late October and full-year results in early February, and those two releases will date this. What would count, stated in advance so it cannot be graded generously later: the manufacturing digital-twin effect reconciled into the cost-of-sales, gross-margin or volume commentary against a named baseline and period; a TuneLab metric with a denominator, partners signed and models in production, offered as an ecosystem KPI; or a LillyPod utilisation or models-in-production figure tied to the R&D line it supports. In the results, not on the Digital and AI page. Lilly has an unusual amount of the raw material for this disclosure, an executive already on record describing an operational effect, and a system behind it. If a company this well equipped can describe the effect to a journalist but not put a number in front of investors, the 2026 disclosure gap is less about capability than about measurement. The test is what can be attributed and defended well enough to file, and Lilly, with more to disclose than most, is the clearest case of whether that threshold is about to be met. On the series' standing question, whether any of these companies could plausibly have an AI-originated medicine approved by 2030, Lilly's own CDO has answered for it: not by 2030, and the people promising sooner are the risk.

text:
By Connor Hart

Eli Lilly reported higher net income and revenue in the recent quarter, fueled by continued surging demand for its GLP-1 weight-loss drugs.

The pharmaceutical company on Wednesday posted second-quarter net income of $7.1 billion, or $7.94 a share, compared with $5.66 billion, or $6.29 a share, a year earlier.

Stripping out one-time items, earnings were $8.38 a share. Analysts surveyed by FactSet expected adjusted earnings of $6.01 a share.

Revenue jumped 48% to $22.97 billion, driven by a 60% increase in volume and partially offset by a 13% decrease in realized prices. Wall Street modeled $20.69 billion in revenue.

The company has seen soaring demand for its weight-loss treatments Mounjaro and Zepbound, both of which saw sales surge from the previous year. The company reported $9.94 billion in Mounjaro revenue--up 91% from last year--as well as $4.93 billion in Zepbound revenue--up 46% from last year.

For the year, Eli Lilly said it now expects adjusted earnings of $35.50 to $36.50 a share, lowering the high-end of its outlook by 50 cents. The company raised its revenue outlook to between $85 billion and $87 billion, from between $82 billion and $85 billion.

Analysts are looking for earnings of $35.04 a share on revenue of $85.28 billion.

Shares rose 5.8%, to $1,180.01, in premarket trading.

The report came as CVS Health separately on Wednesday said it will revamp its weight management program through a partnership with Eli Lilly, allowing patients to use the CVS Health app to view transparent pricing options for GLP-1 treatments.

text:
WPP, one of the world's three largest advertising groups by revenue, posted its biggest single-day stock gain since its 1995 IPO on Thursday after first-half 2026 results landed well ahead of analyst expectations — and provided the clearest evidence yet that the company's AI-driven restructuring is starting to pay off. In London trading, shares surged as much as 30% intraday before settling around 25% higher at 383.6 pence per WPP results filing, while American depositary receipts in New York premarket trading climbed more than 25% to $25.82, approaching the stock's 52-week high of $27.50.

The move reflected something the market had stopped expecting from WPP: a meaningful beat. The company reported headline operating profit of £398 million for the six months ended June 30, 2026 — a figure more than 13% above analyst consensus of approximately £347 million and one that arrived alongside a sharp sequential improvement in the underlying revenue trajectory.

Results That Surprised the Street

Revenue less pass-through costs — WPP's preferred measure of underlying performance, stripping out money it passes directly to media owners on behalf of clients — fell 4.7% on a like-for-like basis to £4.75 billion for the half. That number, while still a decline, came in considerably better than the "mid-to-high single-digit" drop management had guided for in April, and below consensus expectations of roughly a 6.5% fall.

The more compelling story was inside the half. The like-for-like decline in revenue less pass-through costs moderated from 6.7% in Q1 to just 2.8% in Q2 — a sequential improvement driven primarily by stronger performance at WPP Media, easing year-on-year comparisons, and improved client spending from existing customers. Reported operating profit rose 18.1% to £261 million, largely because impairment charges were significantly lower than a year earlier.

Total revenue declined 4.4% on a reported basis to £6.37 billion.

The board maintained the interim dividend at 7.5 pence per share and reaffirmed full-year guidance: headline operating margin of between 12% and 13%, and a continued improvement in the like-for-like trajectory in the second half.

Cindy Rose: Technology CEO Running an Advertising Company

None of this was inevitable — or perhaps even predictable — when Cindy Rose took the helm in September 2025. A former Microsoft UK President, OBE recipient in 2019 for services to the UK technology sector, Rose was the first WPP chief executive drawn from a technology company rather than the advertising industry. That appointment was, in retrospect, a deliberate signal about where the company intended to go.

"I am encouraged by our first-half performance which is in line with our expectations," Rose told analysts on the morning call. "We are firmly on track with Phase 1 of our Elevate28 plan to stabilise the business. Our objective for the first half was to put in place the building blocks of the new organisational structure and this is now complete."

Her plan — unveiled in February 2026 under the name Elevate28 — is the most structurally ambitious restructuring WPP has attempted in its history. It scraps the company's traditional holding company model, under which dozens of independently branded agencies competed for accounts and operated separate profit-and-loss structures, in favor of a single integrated operating company organized across four units: WPP Media, WPP Creative, WPP Production, and the newly launched WPP Enterprise Solutions, which went live on July 1, 2026. The four units span four regions — North America, EMEA, APAC, and LATAM — and are unified through WPP Open, the company's agentic marketing platform.

The cost program attached to the Elevate28 restructuring plan targets £500 million in gross annualized savings by 2028. WPP said Thursday it is on track to deliver £100 million of in-year savings in 2026. The company has also completed more than 15 non-core asset disposals expected to generate over £200 million in proceeds this year, ahead of prior expectations.

How WPP Open Actually Works: Inside the Large Marketing Model

At the heart of the Elevate28 strategy — and the reason WPP's turnaround is a technology story — is WPP Open and its underlying intelligence layer, Open Intelligence.

WPP describes Open Intelligence as a "Large Marketing Model" — a term deliberately chosen in analogy to Large Language Models: where LLMs are trained to predict and generate text from patterns in human language, the LMM is trained to predict audience behavior and marketing performance from patterns in how people engage with content, brands, platforms, and purchase decisions. The distinction matters because it represents a fundamental architectural divergence from how advertising technology has traditionally worked.

The platform's data layer was built on technology from InfoSum, a data collaboration company WPP acquired in April 2025 and integrated into its media unit. InfoSum pioneered "federated" data collaboration — a privacy-preserving architecture in which machine learning models are trained locally on each party's data rather than centralizing raw datasets. The practical result is WPP's claim that the platform connects advertiser data with signals from more than 350 partners — including Google, Meta, Microsoft Advertising, Snap, and TikTok, along with measurement firms Adelaide, Adstra, Circana, Experian, and Lumen Research — without client data ever leaving the advertiser's own secure environment.

The model runs on Google Cloud's Spanner Graph — a globally distributed relational database with native graph query capabilities — which enables real-time relationship queries across behavioral data at the scale WPP's client base requires.

What the Platform Delivered in Q2

In Q2, WPP expanded strategic partnerships with Google, Meta, and AWS to integrate advanced predictive and generative AI tools directly into the platform. The most technically ambitious product to deploy was the Cultural Intelligence Engine — a multimodal, geospatial predictive AI system developed jointly with Google Cloud research partnership that extracts early social signals from public content, clusters them into distinct cultural codes, and forecasts their diffusion across 50 cities and 50 categories.

The engine uses Google Maps Platform's Places Insights and Maps Imagery Grounding to ground cultural trend detection in physical-world context, and was available in-market by Q2. WPP cited a specific result from an earlier phase of the Google partnership: an "Electric Vehicle Readiness Index" for a large automotive client, built using Google Maps Places Insights and Population Dynamics data, that achieved 77% higher campaign performance versus standard designated market area targeting at 15% lower cost-to-conversion.

WPP Open's Agent Hub — an internal app store of AI agents launched in January 2026 that functions as a centralized library encoding decades of WPP's proprietary expertise — had more than 75,000 users across the company's workforce of approximately 100,000 by early 2026.

New Business: Top of the League Table

Perhaps the most closely watched metric under Rose's leadership has been new business performance, and here the results were emphatic. WPP topped J.P. Morgan's net new business rankings for H1 2026 new business table, topping the table for a second consecutive quarter.

Key wins during the period included consolidated mandates from The Estée Lauder Companies, Jaguar Land Rover, Henkel, Airbnb, Wendy's, and Heineken, alongside integrated regional assignments across Latin America, Europe, and Asia Pacific. Key retentions included Skechers, Tesco in the UK and Central Europe, Huawei in China, L'Oréal in Australia and New Zealand, Uber in APAC, and Deutsche Bahn in Germany.

CFO Joanne Wilson cautioned that net new business would remain a drag on revenues in every quarter of 2026, as prior account losses — including significant mandates from Mars and the Coca-Cola US business, both of which migrated to rival Publicis — continue to weigh on reported numbers. However, she said the drag is easing visibly quarter by quarter. Top-25 clients as a group declined 6.3% for the first half but improved to just 3.2% in Q2 — and, excluding the impact of prior-year assignment losses, that group returned to growth in the quarter.

The Publicis Question: A Decade-Long Structural Gap

The market's enthusiasm on Thursday comes with a structural caveat that any honest assessment of WPP's position must name directly.

WPP's Elevate28 strategy — a single integrated operating company organized around four solution hubs, with data and media at the center — is architecturally nearly identical to Publicis Groupe's "Power of One" model, which Publicis began implementing in 2015 and has been executing ever since. Publicis accelerated that integration through its 2019 acquisition of Epsilon (data and identity) and its 2022 acquisition of Profitero (analytics), and announced in May 2026 that it intends to acquire data collaboration platform LiveRamp to deepen its first-party data capabilities further. The result: Publicis surpassed WPP as the world's largest advertising group by revenue in 2024 and is forecasting 4% to 5% organic growth in 2026, while WPP is still reporting a 4.7% decline.

The question the market is now implicitly betting on is whether WPP's AI architecture — specifically, the Large Marketing Model built on InfoSum's federated clean-room infrastructure running on Google Spanner Graph — constitutes a genuinely differentiated capability that Publicis's older data stack cannot easily replicate. LiveRamp, which Publicis is buying, operates through a different technical model: an identity-graph approach that links user identity across disparate datasets. InfoSum's federated architecture avoids centralizing identity data entirely, which proponents argue produces more durable privacy compliance in a post-cookie world. Whether the technical distinction translates into measurable client outcomes is what the next several quarters of results will need to show.

Regional Breakdown: APAC and LATAM Lead Recovery

Across geographies, the picture was nuanced but broadly improving. North America remained the most challenged market, declining 6.0% in H1 and 4.3% in Q2, with declines moderating from the prior-year comparative period. EMEA was down 4.3% for the half and 3.0% in Q2, with declines moderating in the UK and Germany, and both Spain and Italy returning to growth.

APAC was a relative bright spot, declining 3.8% overall for the half but returning to growth of 0.3% in Q2 — with China particularly strong, growing 15.6% in Q2 on the back of timing factors and easier comparisons. LATAM declined just 1.2% for the period and turned positive at 0.9% growth in Q2.

By business unit, WPP Production was the standout, growing 1.6% for the first half and 1.3% in Q2. WPP Media improved from an 8.3% decline in Q1 to a 2.8% decline in Q2. WPP Creative narrowed its decline from 6.3% in Q1 to 3.5% in Q2. Among client sectors, CPG and Tech & Digital Services remained under pressure, each declining around 9% for the half. Healthcare & Pharma, Automotive, and Government all returned to growth in Q2.

Balance Sheet: Debt Coming Down

WPP's balance sheet also showed improvement. Adjusted net debt at June 30, 2026 stood at £2.935 billion, down £326 million from the same point a year earlier, including a £125 million beneficial impact from IFRS 9 accounting amendments. Average adjusted net debt over the past 12 months declined to £3.304 billion from £3.383 billion at end-2025.

WPP continues to target adjusted operating cash flow before working capital of between £800 million and £900 million for the full year.

What Comes Next: A Narrowing Gap and a Structural Test

Looking ahead, management projected continued sequential improvement in H2. WPP expects like-for-like revenue less pass-through costs to decline in the low-to-mid single digits in the second half — an improvement from the first half — with a path toward top-line growth mapped out for 2027 as the "Build" phase of Elevate28 takes effect. Full-year headline operating margin guidance of 12% to 13% was maintained, though management flagged that second-half margins could be up to approximately 200 basis points lower year-on-year, reflecting planned investment in growth initiatives and the rebuilding of incentive structures.

Rose said the company is building an "early-warning system" to identify and respond to client risk — a response to the assignment losses that weighed on the business in 2024 and 2025. WPP Open's data connectivity is central to that retention strategy: the platform's ability to link advertiser data with partner signals in real time means client campaign performance is continuously monitored within WPP's own infrastructure, rather than reviewed quarterly in external reports.

The competitive picture remains demanding. WPP's rival Omnicom completed its $13 billion deal to acquire Interpublic Group in late 2025 and has set a target of reducing staff costs by 10% as part of post-merger integration, creating an enlarged competitor that now competes directly on scale. The long-term risk of disintermediation by hyperscalers — Google, Microsoft, and Amazon all offer AI-native ad management tools that bypass agency intermediaries — remains structural across the industry.

But Thursday's market reaction represented something more specific than sentiment: it reflected a calculation that, for the first time in several years, WPP's trajectory is moving in the right direction and its technical differentiation — built on a Large Marketing Model that its nearest competitors did not have as of the end of Q2 — may be real enough to sustain that direction.

All currency conversions in this article use a GBP/USD rate of approximately $1.33, current as of August 6, 2026; conversions are approximate.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is WPP Open, and why does it matter for the turnaround?

WPP Open is the company's agentic marketing platform — the technological system through which all four of WPP's new operating units (Media, Creative, Production, Enterprise Solutions) are connected and coordinated. Its core is Open Intelligence, a "Large Marketing Model" trained on behavioral and marketing performance data rather than text. The platform connects advertiser data with more than 350 media and data partners through InfoSum's federated clean-room architecture, meaning client data never leaves the advertiser's secure environment. It matters for the turnaround because it is the primary tool WPP is using to differentiate its integrated offer from competitors and to win and retain major mandates — the wins at Estée Lauder, Airbnb, and Heineken cited in Thursday's results were all integrated client relationships managed through WPP Open.

How does WPP compare to Publicis and Omnicom right now?

Publicis Groupe's Power of One strategy helped Publicis surpass WPP as the world's largest advertising group by revenue in 2024 and is currently forecasting 4% to 5% organic growth in 2026, while WPP is still reporting a 4.7% half-year decline. Publicis's advantage traces to its "Power of One" integration strategy, which it began executing in 2015 — a decade before WPP's Elevate28. Omnicom completed its $13 billion acquisition of Interpublic Group in late 2025, creating another enlarged competitor. Elevate28 is WPP CEO Cindy Rose's three-phase restructuring strategy announced in February 2026. Phase 1 (2026) is "Stabilise" — implementing the new four-unit structure, achieving £100 million in cost savings, and completing 15+ non-core asset disposals. Phase 2 (2027) is "Build" — implementing a new go-to-market strategy and targeting a return to organic revenue growth. Phase 3 (2028) is full delivery of £500 million in gross annualized cost savings. As of the H1 2026 results, WPP confirmed Phase 1 is on track.

text:
Adobe’s whole business is the apps creative professionals open every day. This week it put more than 70 of those tools inside a rival’s chatbot. The company has launched a single Adobe plugin for ChatGPT that pulls in Photoshop, Premiere, Lightroom, Illustrator, InDesign, Acrobat, Express, and its Firefly generative models.

It replaces the handful of separate connectors Adobe shipped late last year through OpenAI’s Apps SDK. Now there is one extension, added from ChatGPT’s settings and summoned by typing @Adobe. It is available worldwide from today.

What it actually does

You describe a task in plain language, and the plugin works out which Adobe tools it needs. Then it runs them behind the scenes. You can apply one style across a batch of product photos, resize a design for different platforms, or turn a spreadsheet into an Acrobat PDF. Hand it a long video, and it can cut a highlight reel and reformat it for Shorts, Reels, or TikTok.

You can use the plugin as a guest. Signing in to a Creative Cloud account unlocks more, including saving work across sessions and generating images with Firefly. Adobe says it runs best inside OpenAI’s Codex app and its recently launched Work suite, Engadget reported. How much you can generate depends on your ChatGPT plan.

A tool inside someone else’s front door

The strategy is the real story. The chatbot is becoming the place people start their work, and Adobe would rather be summoned inside ChatGPT than lose the user who never opens Photoshop again. It is meeting people on a rival’s surface before that surface swallows the workflow whole.

Adobe is careful to draw a line.

“We want Adobe’s pro-grade tools for creativity and productivity to be available wherever people work,” said Forest Key, its vice-president of Firefly and agentic AI. The plugin “isn’t a replacement” for the flagship apps, he added, which “go deeper when projects call for hands-on precision”. Speaking to CNET, product lead Deepti Pradeep framed it as an on-ramp back into Adobe’s own apps.

For OpenAI the logic is simpler. Every task it can absorb is a reason not to leave ChatGPT, which feeds its ambition to be the app people never close.

The tightrope

There is a catch, and Adobe names it. The plugin will not deliver pixel-perfect results, Digital Trends noted, and the flagship apps remain the place for precision. There is a harder tension too. Adobe is baking generative AI deeper into its products, through Firefly and new Photoshop assistants, even as many professional creators remain hostile to generative tools.

The company is betting it can be both the chatbot’s creative engine and the professional’s trusted studio. The risk is that the first makes the second feel optional.

GREAT NECK, N.Y., Aug. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Philips International today announced that it has completed the acquisition of the healthcare consulting, technology and recruiting businesses operated by The Nash Group, Inc., Advance Solutions International, Inc. and Nursing Advisory Services LLC.

For more than 30 years, The Nash Group has helped hospitals improve clinical operations, workforce management and financial performance. Its services include healthcare operations consulting, staffing and acuity solutions, hospital technology, and domestic and international nurse recruitment.

"The Nash businesses have built valuable expertise, longstanding relationships and differentiated solutions addressing operational and workforce challenges in healthcare," said Adrian Miller, Managing Director, Corporate M&A at Philips International. "Our clients will receive the same commitment to excellence they have trusted for 30 years, now supported by enhanced technology, stronger recruitment infrastructure and deeper operational capacity."

The acquisition provides Philips International with an established healthcare services and technology platform. Philips plans to invest in people, technology, business development capabilities and operating infrastructure while the Nash team remains focused on serving customers and expanding market reach.

Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed.

name: UniCredit
title: Commerzbank Opens UniCredit Merger Talks After 94% Profit Surge Sets Asking Price
description:
Operating profit for the quarter reached €1.37 billion (approximately $1.58 billion), up 17% year-on-year, as total revenues expanded 9% to €3.30 billion (approximately $3.81 billion).
Net commission income climbed 7.2% to €1.08 billion (approximately $1.25 billion), while net interest income held broadly stable at €2.06 billion (approximately $2.38 billion) for the quarter.
For the first half of 2026, Commerzbank posted record net profit of €1.8 billion (approximately $2.08 billion), up 40% from the prior-year period.
The bank also announced a €1.2 billion (approximately $1.39 billion) share buyback — pending approval from Germany's Finance Agency — and reaffirmed its full-year capital return target of approximately €3.2 billion (approximately $3.69 billion) through buybacks and dividends.
Frequently Asked Questions What conditions has Commerzbank CEO Bettina Orlopp set for a merger with UniCredit?
text:
Germany's Commerzbank formally opened merger negotiations with Italy's UniCredit on Thursday, August 6 — the same morning it reported a 94% surge in second-quarter net profit, a strategic double-play that transformed Germany's second-largest private bank from a cornered acquisition target into a willing negotiator with an unusually strong hand.

"We have started talks on this, which is in the genuine interest of both UniCredit and Commerzbank, as we are both determined to create value for our shareholders, clients and employees," CEO Bettina Orlopp told analysts. "I'm optimistic that, step by step, we can find common ground on governance and also on the business model."

The announcement ended nearly two years of fierce German resistance to UniCredit's creeping advance — and it landed alongside one of the strongest quarterly performances in Commerzbank's 156-year history, framing Frankfurt's capitulation as a negotiated entry rather than a surrender.

Record Quarter Becomes Orlopp's Opening Bid

Commerzbank's Q2 2026 net profit surged 94% year-on-year to €898 million (approximately $1.04 billion), beating the analyst consensus of €845 million (approximately $976 million) and marking a record operating profit for any single quarter in the bank's history. Operating profit for the quarter reached €1.37 billion (approximately $1.58 billion), up 17% year-on-year, as total revenues expanded 9% to €3.30 billion (approximately $3.81 billion).

Net commission income climbed 7.2% to €1.08 billion (approximately $1.25 billion), while net interest income held broadly stable at €2.06 billion (approximately $2.38 billion) for the quarter. For the first half of 2026, Commerzbank posted record net profit of €1.8 billion (approximately $2.08 billion), up 40% from the prior-year period.

The bank also announced a €1.2 billion (approximately $1.39 billion) share buyback — pending approval from Germany's Finance Agency — and reaffirmed its full-year capital return target of approximately €3.2 billion (approximately $3.69 billion) through buybacks and dividends. Its Common Equity Tier 1 capital buffer remained robust at 14.4%, and its net return on tangible equity of 12.6% was described by the company as a record result.

For shareholders and investors tracking the takeover saga, the financial message was clear: any UniCredit valuation for Commerzbank will now be measured against a bank growing its profits, not defending its survival.

What Orlopp Is Demanding — and Why It Matters

Despite opening the negotiating door, Orlopp made two conditions explicit, and they are not cosmetic. First, Commerzbank must retain a separate stock-market listing in Frankfurt. Second, UniCredit cannot "unilaterally decide on fundamental structural measures" even if the Italian lender acquires a majority stake ahead of Commerzbank's next annual shareholder meeting.

"This creates a clear responsibility for both sides," Orlopp said on the earnings call. "It requires a shared understanding of the business model and the involvement of all stakeholders."

The structural condition has real teeth under German corporate law: a full operational merger of Commerzbank into UniCredit, or a combination with UniCredit's German subsidiary HypoVereinsbank, would require a 75% supermajority at a shareholders' meeting — a threshold UniCredit cannot clear unilaterally even at nearly 50% economic interest. UniCredit itself acknowledged this constraint in an official statement, noting in an official UniCredit statement that "the only matters requiring a 75% majority at a shareholders' meeting would be a merger or other corporate reorganization matters."

This is the legal architecture that turns Orlopp's conditions from aspirational demands into genuine negotiating levers.

Nearly Two Years in the Making

The Thursday announcement closed the curtain on a corporate brinkmanship campaign that began in September 2024, when UniCredit CEO Andrea Orcel quietly outbid rivals in a German government sale of Commerzbank shares, acquiring a 4.5% stake that, combined with a prior open-market purchase, gave the Milan-based lender a sudden 9% foothold. German officials labeled the move a "hostile attack" on national financial sovereignty.

By March 2025, the European Central Bank had granted UniCredit approval to lift its stake to 29.9%. In March 2026, Orcel escalated further, launching a formal voluntary exchange offer under German takeover law (WpÜG) valued at approximately €35 billion (approximately $40.4 billion) at launch — a figure analysts have estimated could reach €45 billion (approximately $52 billion) accounting for UniCredit's full position.

Commerzbank's board rejected the offer in April 2026 as "financially inadequate" with a "vague plan" carrying "considerable execution risks." When the acceptance period closed on July 3, 2026, only about 17.6% of Commerzbank shares had been tendered — and Commerzbank's own shareholder tracking showed that fewer than 2% of independent institutional and retail investors accepted the offer. Tendered shares predominantly came from banks and parties connected to UniCredit, and the bank noted an unusual surge in securities lending activity that it said raised questions about whether beneficial owners had knowingly consented to the tendering of their shares.

With UniCredit controlling approximately 47.6% of Commerzbank's capital — translating to roughly 49.7% of voting rights once Commerzbank's own treasury shares are excluded — and the Frankfurt public prosecutor having declined to open a market-manipulation inquiry in July, the Italian bank had effectively reached a stalemate: it controlled nearly half the shareholder register but lacked the supermajority needed to force structural change. The pivot to formal talks was the logical next step.

The Stakes for Commerzbank's 10 Million Customers and 40,000 Employees

For readers with accounts at Commerzbank or business relationships with the bank, the negotiated merger path is better news than the hostile alternative — but it is not cost-free. Commerzbank has already announced 6,900 cumulative defensive job cuts across two restructuring rounds in 2025 and 2026, against a workforce that stood at approximately 40,000 at the start of the year. Germany's banking union ver.di has estimated that a UniCredit-driven integration could put 10,000 Commerzbank positions at risk, particularly in IT, administration, and back-office functions.

A merger between Commerzbank and HypoVereinsbank — UniCredit's existing German subsidiary, with approximately €263.5 billion ($304.4 billion) in total assets — is not expected to proceed until after Commerzbank has been "strengthened and transformed," per UniCredit's own public statements. When it does, the combined entity would become Germany's second-largest private lender after Deutsche Bank and, measured by total assets, potentially the eurozone's largest bank.

Commerzbank describes itself as "the leading financier of the German Mittelstand" — the ecosystem of family-owned small and medium-sized enterprises that account for more than 99% of German businesses, roughly 60% of private-sector employment, and 68% of Germany's exports. Former Supervisory Board Chairman Jens Weidmann, who opposed the takeover, warned that HypoVereinsbank and Bank Austria — both absorbed into UniCredit in 2005 — provide a cautionary template: their German and Austrian footprints shrank after integration.

Commerzbank's AI Bet Is Now the Negotiating Table

Commerzbank's standalone argument has an increasingly concrete technological dimension. Its "Momentum 2030" strategy commits approximately €600 million (approximately $693 million) in cumulative AI investments between 2026 and 2030, targeting a 70% reduction in some operating costs, a 20% revenue uplift, and improved risk controls. Its virtual retail banking assistant "Ava" now handles approximately 30,000 customer inquiries per month, with more than 70% resolved autonomously, and the bank has deployed AI in partnership with fraud-detection firm Hawk to tackle money laundering.

For UniCredit, which must now negotiate the value of that AI investment into any deal structure, this is no longer a bank defending past profits — it is a bank arguing the current share price undervalues a digital transformation still in progress. Whether that argument holds up in negotiations is what the coming months will determine.

Road Ahead: ECB, Capital Costs, and a Cautious Rating Agency

The path to a completed merger remains lined with regulatory and political hurdles. The ECB has yet to grant formal approval for UniCredit's acquisition of controlling interest — a decision expected in the fourth quarter of 2026. UniCredit CEO Orcel has publicly targeted Q4 2026 as his completion window, with the qualifier "maybe later" acknowledging the persistent uncertainty that has defined the saga throughout.

S&P Global Ratings affirmed Commerzbank's long-term issuer credit rating at "A" but cut its outlook from "positive" to "stable" in July 2026, citing a specific risk: a full operational absorption into UniCredit could strip Commerzbank of the independent capital buffers that had previously positioned it for a potential upgrade. The agency's caution stands in deliberate contrast to the equity market's enthusiasm: Commerzbank shares have risen approximately 8% since the start of 2026, touching a 52-week high of €39.72 (approximately $45.86) in mid-July.

Germany's federal government, which still holds a 12% stake in Commerzbank, has softened its position under Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who stated publicly that Berlin would not block a merger in principle — but the government has not tendered its shares, and Hesse's state premier Boris Rhein has separately called for guarantees on headquarters and employment.

Banking Union's Biggest Test

Beyond the corporate scoreboard, the Commerzbank-UniCredit saga has become the definitive stress test of the EU's twelve-year-old Banking Union — the reform framework built after the 2008 financial crisis to enable the kind of cross-border bank consolidation that would make European institutions competitive with American and Chinese giants. The ECB has consistently and publicly supported the deal on those grounds; ECB supervisory officials have argued that completing the Banking Union — including through cross-border mergers of significant institutions — is essential to keeping European banks globally relevant.

Yet the resistance from Berlin underscored how politically fraught that vision remains when national financial champions are the target. Legal scholars at Maastricht University have argued that Germany's conduct in opposing the takeover may be in tension with EU capital movement rules — the same rules the Banking Union was designed to give practical force.

If formal talks now produce a deal on terms both Frankfurt and Milan can accept, they will have done more than create a large bank. They will have demonstrated that the Banking Union's framework for cross-border consolidation actually functions — setting precedent for further eurozone integration. If talks collapse, the reverse lesson will be equally clear: that national political resistance can outlast even a near-majority shareholder position and render the Banking Union's consolidation promise theoretical.

For Orlopp, Thursday's dual-header — a record profit quarter and a formal seat at the negotiating table — represents the strongest possible position from which to shape that outcome in Commerzbank's interest. Whether the final terms protect a separate Frankfurt listing, shield Mittelstand lending relationships, and preserve enough of the AI-led "Momentum 2030" strategy to justify the deal will be the test of whether two years of fierce resistance produced a better outcome than capitulation would have.

Frequently Asked Questions

What conditions has Commerzbank CEO Bettina Orlopp set for a merger with UniCredit?

Orlopp has stated two explicit conditions in connection with opening formal talks: Commerzbank must retain a separate stock-market listing in Frankfurt, and UniCredit cannot unilaterally impose "fundamental structural measures" — including a merger with HypoVereinsbank — even if it acquires a majority position. Under German corporate law, a formal merger or major reorganization requires a 75% supermajority at a shareholders' meeting, a threshold UniCredit cannot reach alone even at approximately 50% economic interest. Orlopp has also indicated both banks would explore potential cost savings and large investment programs jointly before any structural combination would be considered.

Will the ECB approve UniCredit's acquisition of control in Commerzbank?

The European Central Bank has not yet issued its formal approval for UniCredit's acquisition of controlling interest in Commerzbank. A decision is expected in the fourth quarter of 2026. The ECB has historically and publicly supported European cross-border bank consolidation as a way to build institutions that can compete with American and Asian rivals. However, the ECB's approval may come with capital requirements attached — potentially raising the cost of the acquisition to UniCredit and complicating the deal's economics. S&P Global Ratings flagged this specific risk when it cut Commerzbank's credit outlook to "stable" in July 2026, warning that a full operational absorption could erode Commerzbank's independent capital buffers.

What does the UniCredit-Commerzbank merger mean for Commerzbank's employees and small business customers?

The employment picture is the most concrete consumer concern. Commerzbank has already cut approximately 6,900 positions in two defensive restructuring rounds since early 2025. Ver.di, Germany's banking union, estimates that a UniCredit-driven integration could put 10,000 Commerzbank jobs at risk — particularly in IT, administration, and back-office roles. For small and medium-sized business customers, the risk is more structural than immediate: Commerzbank has long positioned itself as the primary lender to Germany's Mittelstand — the family-owned small and medium enterprise ecosystem that employs roughly 60% of the German private-sector workforce and generates 68% of the country's exports. Critics of the deal, including former Supervisory Board Chairman Jens Weidmann, have pointed to the evolution of HypoVereinsbank and Bank Austria after their 2005 absorption into UniCredit as evidence that German and Austrian banking footprints tend to shrink under Milan's ownership.

Why does this merger matter beyond Germany and Italy — and what is the EU Banking Union?

The EU Banking Union is a post-2008 reform framework designed to create unified financial supervision across the eurozone, enabling banks from different member states to merge and operate across borders as seamlessly as domestic institutions do. The European Central Bank directly supervises significant banks under this framework — known as the Single Supervisory Mechanism — and has long argued that cross-border consolidation is necessary to build European banks large enough to compete globally. The UniCredit-Commerzbank negotiation is widely regarded as the most important test of whether that consolidation goal is achievable in practice: if the deal closes on negotiated terms, it sets precedent for further eurozone banking integration. If it fails under political pressure, it will confirm that national governments can effectively veto the Banking Union's consolidation promise regardless of the regulatory framework in place.

text:
The threat posed by attackers using AI to enhance their offensive activities, and the need for defenders to use AI to combat those activities, has been a major focus of our analysis in 2026.

New data from IBM quantifies the financial impact of AI-powered attacks, how AI can lessen that impact, and how AI-powered defenses can protect against the uninformed use of AI – or shadow AI – by a company’s own workers.

The 2026 Data Breach Report from IBM presents data from 600+ organizations across 17 industries and 16 geographic regions; it provides valuable insights into the rapidly shifting security challenges facing business leaders, and the increasingly powerful defenses at their disposal.

In this report, I’ll present what I find to be five of the most compelling findings through an AI lens, but I recommend reviewing the full report, which is packed with fresh insight.

Breach Cost By Industry

Tech analysts widely cite a few industries as having the most valuable — and sensitive — data to maintain and protect. And the findings in this report on the cost of data breaches aligns closely with those long-held views.

Overall, the study found that the global average cost of a data breach — across industries— reached $5 million last year, an increase of 12% vs. 2025. The report notes that 63% of those costs — nearly two–thirds — are from two functions: 1) detection and escalation and 2) lost business. As I reported earlier this week, detection and escalation are being addressed by the cybersecurity community broadly.

Even more insightful is the breakdown of breach cost by industry, where healthcare leads the way with an average cost of $6.6 million in 2026, which, interestingly, is down from over $7 million in 2025. “Attackers continue to value and target the industry’s patient PII, which can be used for identity theft, insurance fraud and other financial crimes,” the report says. Personally Identifiable Information (PII) includes data such as tax ID numbers, emails, and home addresses.

Healthcare is followed in breach costs by financial services, with a per-breach cost of $6.3 million in 2026, up 11% from $5.6 million in 2025. In all of the other top 10 industries by breach costs, the cost per incident increased in 2026.

The most stolen or compromised data type, at 52% of the total, was customer PII and the cost of those PII compromises averages $192 per record.

Average Data Breach Cost by Industry, in Millions

Also notable: costs escalate when attacks leverage AI; those powered by AI average $6 million per breach, vs. $5 million for those that aren’t AI driven. The most common type of AI attack (45%): deepfake or impersonation attacks.

Recovery Time Factors

Once a data breach occurs, it’s clear that companies continue to struggle to recover. Just 42% of companies report they have fully recovered from a breach and among those that have recovered, 71% need 100 days or more to do so. That’s a protracted recovery time, if recovery happens at all, highlighting again how damaging breaches can be.

Time For Organizations to Fully Recover from Data Breaches

Going on Offense

Given the severity and impact of data breaches, it may come as a surprise that organizations are not extensively using AI to protect their data – yet. A little over one third of respondents — 36% in 2026 – report extensive use of AI, up more than 10% from one year ago. But 25% still report no use of AI in security measures – lack of trust in AI is likely one important factor in this limited-use finding.

Percent of organizations in each category of Defensive AI use

There’s hard financial data in support of using AI defensively: a nearly $2 million cost per breach savings for those that use AI extensively. The average cost is $4 million for AI users and nearly $6 million for non-users.

Where AI Is Being Used

The aforementioned AI security leaders (in deployment terms) are focusing their efforts on AI agents that perform threat hunting (54%) and automated response/containment (54%), followed by alert triage (45%). All three functions are frequently cited by security and tech pros as major stress points with a strong propensity to overwhelm human security analysts, so this finding underscores how the human capacity problem can be addressed with AI.

Use of AI Agents by Security Function

AI In The Shadows

The final data point we’ll highlight revolves around shadow AI — the practice of employees using unauthorized, typically free, tools to do their work without an organization’s approval or knowledge. It could also include individually created AI agents that, without proper guardrails, could wreak havoc or open the door to data breaches.

This phenomenon, which mirrors shadow IT as well as past struggles with personal cell phones for corporate functions, has given rise to vendor initiatives aimed at providing inventories or ideally, complete visibility, into the AI tools in use within a company.

The data breach report hones in specifically on the impact of a shadow AI-driven security incident, showing data loss and operational disruption as the downsides impacting the most companies — and with more companies reporting those outcomes in 2026 vs. 2025.

Companies Reporting Each Shadow AI Security Incident Impact

AI is presenting new opportunities to combat bad actors and misguided employees, but it’s clear companies are in a race to keep up with the AI-driven activities of those groups. The data breach report overall could be considered mildly encouraging in that it shows AI being used defensively is putting up important wins. But not enough companies are availing themselves of the technology – or they aren’t yet confident enough in the technology to this point – to truly turn the tide.
