The finance department increasingly has the mandate to help leadership act while the outcome can still change. Within OpenAI’s finance department, led by CFO Sarah Friar, there is a strategic finance team that functions as a cross-functional partner to product, partnerships, engineering, and go-to-market teams. The team’s tool of choice is ChatGPT Work, an agent that can act across apps and files, stay on a task for hours, and turn a goal into a finished product.

The webinar was led by three members of OpenAI’s strategic finance team: Stephanie Struck, head of product finance; Kyle Kober, director of product finance; and Jackson Wang, who leads data science. “Our entire finance department uses ChatGPT Work,” Kober said. Teams combine approved financial data, Excel models, and business context to get frontier-level intelligence that completes tasks two to three times faster, he said.

Struck demonstrated the tool auditing quarter-end materials to catch discrepancies between board decks and actuals. Wang described shifting forecasting “from more of a spreadsheet-based system to more of a statistical-based forecasting model,” improving both accuracy and collaboration. They detailed how the tool automates monthly close by pulling data from systems like Databricks into one validated dashboard. ChatGPT Work speeds up and structures the close, but doesn’t replace the underlying accounting system or a controller’s sign-off.

Newer features include dynamic slide editing, a finance assistant for quick questions, an on-the-go podcast, with a “CFO spotlight” that surfaces the month’s top priorities and biggest variances—a feature the presenters said Friar values.

Regarding data governance, Kober said: “All of it is governed and auditable with controls to lock down the spend and the usage of your ChatGPT work experience.” However, there wasn’t much discussion of who owns the data, or how agent decisions get audited.

The skills that matter now

Struck addressed what OpenAI looks for in finance hires. Accounting, forecasting, controls, and analytical rigor are still required, she said, but they’re now baseline, not differentiators. What sets people apart is comfort with data and AI tools paired with judgment: knowing which questions to ask, challenging an AI’s output, and translating it into a business implication. “Why does this matter for the business?” is the question she wants her team asking constantly. Equally critical is communication—insights only matter, Struck said, if they’re shared quickly enough to change how the organization actually operates.

It seems that OpenAI isn’t betting that the tool alone gets this right. It’s betting on people who know when to push back on what it says.

Sheryl Estrada

Sheryl.Estrada@fortune.com

Leaderboard

Kevin Kalicak was appointed CFO and treasurer of Portillo’s (Nasdaq: PTLO), the fast-casual restaurant known for serving Chicago-style favorites, effective Sept. 7. Kalicak has decades of financial leadership experience within the restaurant industry, serving in various roles with Darden Restaurants for more than 25 years. Most recently, Kalicak served as SVP of finance for Olive Garden. He has held several positions across various areas of brand finance, business analytics, enterprise finance, and investor relations within Darden’s portfolio.

Carla Chiorazzo was appointed CFO of Adolfson & Peterson Construction, a national construction management and contracting firm. Chiorazzo brings more than 20 years of financial and operational leadership experience. She most recently served as CFO of Conti Federal, a federal construction and design-build company. Before that, she was VP of finance, shared services at PAE, where she supported finance processes for more than 15,000 employees.

Big Deal

Gen Z has the lowest savings-to-spending ratio of any generation—and yet they're spending more, not less. A new Bank of America Institute report finds that despite tight budgets, Gen Z's discretionary spending on beauty, jewelry, coffee, and travel has actually strengthened over the past six months, defying the "K-shaped" pattern seen elsewhere in the economy.

The catch: a tougher labor market for new entrants is pushing more of them into gig work to fund it, with nearly 40% of that gig income now coming through social commerce platforms, according to the report.

Going deeper

"How credit risk is factored in corporate bond spreads" is a report in Wharton's business journal. A new Wharton paper aims to resolve a long-standing bond market puzzle: credit spreads have implied investors should earn healthy compensation for risk, yet realized returns since 1986 have often disappointed despite historically moderate defaults. Using 128 years of data, researchers trace this to two culprits—an unrepresentative recent sample and a benchmarking bias from mismatching callable bonds to Treasuries—and find the credit risk premium is real once corrected. For CFOs, that's a clearer signal on whether current spreads reflect true borrowing risk or a measurement quirk when timing debt issuance.

Overheard

“We’re taking a small amount of the expertise that we use for rockets and satellites, and applying that to scaling terrestrial data centers.”

From a stock price perspective, Uber Technologies (UBER -5.29%) has struggled this year. Shares are down 20% year-to-date.

From a business perspective, however, things seem to be going quite well. The company reported earnings on Aug. 5, and many experts were impressed by the results. Uber struggled to achieve profitability in its early years. But the company has been consistently profitable over the last two years.

Uber’s core business isn’t very capital intensive. Its drivers are typically the ones purchasing and maintaining their equipment. That has allowed higher earnings to translate into higher cash flows.

“[T]railing twelve-month free cash flow exceeded $10 billion for the first time in Uber’s history,” Uber announced, “giving us the flexibility to both invest for the future and pursue strategic opportunities, while continuing to reduce our share count.”

Where exactly will Uber be investing its new cash? There’s one obvious answer: robotaxis.

Can Uber dominate the robotaxi market?

text:
The AI world is looking to D.C. for clarity.

On Tuesday, staffers from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and other tech companies convened in Washington to review the administration's new framework for reviewing advanced AI models. Now, the rest of the industry eagerly awaits answers on what will be included in the framework — a structured way for President Donald Trump's administration to evaluate AI models' cyber capabilities.

The framework represents a turning point for AI oversight. While Trump's administration has adopted a light-touch regulatory approach, rapid advances in AI models for cybersecurity and hacking are beginning to upend it.

It's an open question how the new process will shape up and affect the release and adoption of new AI models. The New York Times reported on Tuesday that White House officials said at the meeting that the federal government plans to review only certain types of AI models from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI for potential security risks and does not plan to review open-source AI models so far, though these plans could change as the technology advances. Open-source models allow anyone to download or modify the code for free.

An executive order in early June directed officials to develop a "benchmarking process to assess the advanced cyber capabilities of AI models" within 60 days. The deadline has passed.

Here are the major outstanding questions.

How committed is the Trump administration to its stance on AI?

The administration's AI oversight approach has been defined by its light-touch regulatory stance. Its AI Action Plan, released in 2025, said that regulation might end up "paralyzing" the industry, and called on agencies to "dismantle unnecessary regulatory barriers that hinder the private sector."

The executive order in June acknowledged a new reality in which AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI have shown marked improvements in coding, finding cybersecurity exploits, and working on longer-term tasks.

The framework, as sketched in the June order, will require companies to share their AI models with the government for up to 30 days before releasing them to the public, giving the government a head start in assessing their cyber capabilities.

Crucially, Trump's executive order described the framework as "voluntary," though it's an open question how the administration would treat companies that skip the process. Jessica Ji, an analyst at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology, said it seems like officials are trying to create a "soft compliance regime."

"Ideally, they can say we're not regulating, this is a voluntary program, but all of the companies whose models they think present potential national security risks would comply," she said.

Which AI models will the framework cover?

Regulating AI is tricky. Rules could target the top-tier labs, specific products, or individual AI models. If regulators home in on the models, more questions pop up. Do they base their rules on the models' size, or when they're released, or what they're capable of?

The conversation in D.C. over recent months has turned around the AI models' capabilities because of new developments like Anthropic's Mythos model and OpenAI's security incident with the AI company Hugging Face.

Trump's executive order asked his agencies to develop a definition of the "covered frontier models" that would be vetted by his administration. Chinese open-source and open-weight models, which have sparked furor in the industry recently because of their advanced capabilities, are almost certainly part of the Tuesday conversation, Ji said.

She added that figuring out ways to categorize AI models is a crucial step for the rulemakers.

What authority will the government have over the leading AI juggernauts?

It's unclear so far how the framework will affect the rollout of AI models, especially if it truly feels voluntary to companies. Ji said she's curious whether there will be any clear guidance on what the administration can do if it finds a dangerous capability while testing unreleased technology.

In June, Trump's Commerce Department responded to cybersecurity concerns about an Anthropic model by issuing an export control that barred the company from granting foreign nationals access. Anthropic ended up pulling down all access to the model until it reached a deal with the administration.

Ji said it's unlikely the administration would keep resorting to export controls, though it's unclear what other levers they might pull to intervene in a model release or to pressure a company to change its product.

She said the meeting will provide more clarity on who in the Trump administration makes the decisions around AI oversight and cybersecurity.

"We're trying to figure out who are the new kind of power players, who has influence in the administration on this set of issues, right now," Ji said.

Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Business Insider.

text:
This sponsored content was created in collaboration with a Skift partner.

Credit card travel programs are becoming a more influential part of how travelers discover, evaluate, and book trips. Skift Research found that credit card rewards programs now match, and in some cases exceed, the perceived value of traditional airline and hotel loyalty programs across major travel markets. In the U.S., 34% of travelers surveyed said credit card programs offer the most rewarding benefits, compared with 22% for hotel programs and 21% for airlines.

That shift helps explain why leading travel credit cards have built curated hotel and lodging programs around more than points. For premium cardholders, the value is increasingly tied to access, benefits, guidance, and a more considered way to choose where to stay.

Inside the Premier and Lifestyle Collections

Capital One Travel has applied that thinking to its Premier and Lifestyle Collections, which launched in 2023 as a lodging extension of the company’s premium travel strategy. The collections give eligible cardholders access to handpicked hotels, resorts, and vacation rentals, with enhanced benefits such as experience credits and room upgrades. The Premier Collection focuses on luxury properties with elevated service and bespoke amenities, while the Lifestyle Collection emphasizes design-forward, locally rooted stays with a distinctive sense of place.

Since launch, the collections have expanded to more than 1,400 properties, reflecting Capital One Travel’s ambition to create a more discerning hotel portfolio that helps cardholders discover distinctive stays and design a trip tailored to their needs. The strategy builds on the premium foundation established with its Venture X card and first airport lounge in late 2021, extending the Capital One Travel experience for eligible cardholders through a vetted collection that adds more guidance and value to choosing where to stay.

“Luxury has become an individualized definition, and our role is to curate experiences that help travelers discover what luxury means to them,” said Phillip LaRue, head of luxury travel at Capital One. “By highlighting diverse properties, our curated portfolio delivers a powerful sense of discovery to cardholders.”

Redefining Premium Travel Through Curation

Curation gives structure to a category that has become increasingly personal. The Premier and Lifestyle Collections are designed to help cardholders move from a wide field of options to a more focused set of stays selected for service, character, and relevance to the trip.

“Today’s travelers are increasingly seeking experiences that feel authentic, memorable, and tailored to their interests rather than simply choosing the most expensive option available,” LaRue said. For Capital One Travel, that creates a role for the Premier and Lifestyle Collections that goes beyond access to inventory. “Our Premier and Lifestyle Collections act as an expert travel curator when planning trips,” he said.

The portfolios include distinctive independent and lifestyle properties, as well as partnerships with groups such as Small Luxury Hotels of the World and The Leading Hotels of the World, alongside established luxury brands such as Belmond, Peninsula, and Six Senses, as well as a growing set of Accor brands, including Fairmont and Raffles. The emphasis, though, is less on the length of the list than on its range. In Puerto Rico, for example, the Premier Collection includes Fairmont El San Juan, a heritage luxury property, while the Lifestyle Collection includes Hotel El Convento, an independent boutique hotel set in one of San Juan’s most historic buildings. Both are elevated stays, but each offers a different expression of the destination.

Building a More Bespoke Premium Portfolio

Behind the collections is a selection process that combines customer insight, partner evaluation, and ongoing quality control. The goal is not to apply a single definition of luxury across every market, but to identify properties that deliver strong hospitality while adding something distinctive to the portfolio.

“Our curation process combines data-driven analysis with a highly selective qualitative review,” said Hya Valdez, head of luxury travel business development and strategic partnerships at Capital One Travel. “We spend significant time understanding a property’s unique story and what distinguishes it within its market while evaluating whether it aligns with the type of experiences our cardholders are seeking.”

Capital One Travel considers guest satisfaction, service quality, amenities, location, operational consistency, and overall guest experience. Once a property joins the portfolio, the team continues to monitor performance and work with hotel and vacation rental partners to ensure the experience continues to meet its standards and the evolving needs of the premium traveler.

Scaling a Collection Built for Discovery

The Premier and Lifestyle Collections have scaled quickly, but the company frames that growth as intentional rather than volume-driven. As more hotels and travel suppliers compete for premium travelers, curated distribution can create new discovery pathways for properties with strong service models, clear stories, and a defined sense of place.

“The growth has been driven by a combination of strong traveler demand, positive partner engagement, and a deliberate strategy to expand thoughtfully across destinations and travel styles,” LaRue said.

For hotel partners, the distinction is both commercial and editorial. A property does not only need to be bookable. It needs to be understandable within the context of the trip a traveler wants to take. A glamping retreat, for example, isn’t competing directly with a five-star city hotel. Each serves a different travel moment, and the role of curation is to help travelers find the property that best matches the experience they’re looking for.

How Lifestyle Stays Complement the Premium Portfolio

Lifestyle-driven hotels have become a bigger part of the premium travel landscape as travelers seek stronger design, deeper local context, and a clearer point of view. Skift Advisory research found that travelers are willing to pay a 40% premium for unique, distinctive local experiences over standard accommodation quality, helping explain why major hotel groups are investing more heavily in lifestyle brands.

For Capital One Travel, the Lifestyle Collection plays a different role inside the broader portfolio. It gives cardholders another way into a destination, one shaped less by traditional luxury cues and more by the culture, design, and neighborhood context around the stay.

“Independent and distinctive properties often provide the type of authentic, locally connected experiences that many travelers are increasingly seeking,” Valdez said. “These hotels frequently have a strong sense of place, unique design perspectives, and highly personalized service models that create memorable stays.”

Valdez pointed to the Lifestyle Collection as a place where local identity can become part of the guest experience rather than a decorative layer added after the fact. Brands such as Bunkhouse Hotels and Ash Hotels, she said, are examples of properties “embedding travelers directly into the neighborhood fabric by integrating local-favorite culinary, art, and music as part of the guest experience.”

More Ways to Experience In-Demand Destinations

As traveler expectations become more personal, destination strategy is becoming part of how Capital One Travel helps cardholders discover what luxury means to them. In markets with strong demand, the goal is to offer a range of stays that can support different trip occasions, from established resorts to lifestyle-led hotels and all-inclusive experiences.

For example, in Riviera Maya, Capital One Travel has expanded its portfolio with Accor and Ennismore properties, including Fairmont Mayakoba, Banyan Tree Mayakoba, and the all-inclusive SLS Playa Mujeres. Together, those additions show how one destination can support several expressions of luxury, giving cardholders more ways to choose a stay that fits the trip they want to take.

The hotel collections also sit within Capital One Travel’s connected travel experience, which spans booking, airport hospitality through Capital One Lounges and Landings, entertainment benefits, and other travel partnerships.

Expanding the Definition of Premium Stays

The strategy extends into experiential lodging, where Capital One Travel is adding properties that meet travelers in less conventional settings. Capital One Travel’s luxury trend research found that 93% of premium spenders are interested in non-traditional stays such as glamping, underscoring how far the definition of premium travel has expanded beyond traditional hotels and resorts.

Under Canvas is one example, bringing premium tent accommodations near national parks into the portfolio.

“Partnerships like Under Canvas, a leader in upscale outdoor hospitality, are a great example of how premium travel is expanding beyond the traditional definition,” Valdez said. “Experiential travel is no longer confined to luxury hotels — it can also be found in extraordinary settings that deliver comfort, service, and memorable experiences in a different way.”

Building a Trusted Filter for Luxury Travel

What distinguishes Capital One Travel’s approach is not only the size of the portfolio, but the work required to keep it relevant as premium travel evolves. As the Premier and Lifestyle Collections grow, the team continues to source the world for exceptional properties and work with hotel and vacation rental partners to ensure the collections continue to reflect what cardholders are looking for.

That makes curation an ongoing discipline rather than a one-time selection process. As traveler expectations evolve, Capital One Travel continues to assess where the collections can offer greater relevance across areas such as wellness, outdoor hospitality, culinary experiences, entertainment, and local connection.

For cardholders, that consistency is what turns a collection into something more useful than a long list of options. As premium travel becomes more varied, the Premier and Lifestyle Collections are designed to grow with a clear point of view and a continued focus on relevance. They become a trusted filter for helping travelers navigate an increasingly diverse premium market.

name: Nvidia
title: Nvidia bankrolls its rivals - Axios
description:
State of play: Nvidia is the largest corporate venture investor in AI by deal value, according to PitchBook research viewed by Axios.
Follow the money: If AI demand continues to outstrip available compute, alternative chips could expand the overall market without damaging Nvidia.
OpenAI still relies on Nvidia chips for training, but has released its own chip for servicing AI queries and recently hired a compute executive, potentially indicating bigger ambitions.
Zoom out: Nvidia currently owns the market for training AI models, according to Jay Goldberg, the lone Wall Street analyst with a sell rating on Nvidia.
In that world, demand for inference chips that are used to run AI models could outpace demand for training chips that Nvidia specializes in.
text:
Nvidia is weighing more than $750 billion in AI investments, financing deals and partnerships — betting that any growth in the compute market will ultimately benefit its chip business.

Why it matters: The world's most valuable chip company is bankrolling the same customers racing to build alternatives to its chips.

State of play: Nvidia is the largest corporate venture investor in AI by deal value, according to PitchBook research viewed by Axios.

Nvidia invests across several AI labs because it doesn't care which model company wins as long as it buys Nvidia's GPUs, per PitchBook.

Bloomberg reports that Nvidia is involved in proposed AI partnerships and financing arrangements valued at more than $750 billion, although only a portion would represent capital directly at risk for Nvidia.

Nvidia is also discussing a guarantee of as much as $250 billion for an OpenAI data center project, reported by the Wall Street Journal, which helps lower OpenAI's borrowing costs, but exposes Nvidia if that debt isn't repaid.

Between the lines: Nvidia is throwing money at companies that could end up being competitors.

"Somebody's going to start competing with them," Jay Hatfield, chief investment officer of QVOL, told Axios.

Follow the money: If AI demand continues to outstrip available compute, alternative chips could expand the overall market without damaging Nvidia.

More capacity could lower AI costs, increase usage and create additional demand for Nvidia's systems.

But if Nvidia helps finance more capacity than the market can absorb, it could face weaker chip pricing, slower orders and losses on guarantees or investments.

Friction point: Many of Nvidia's biggest customers are building chips designed to peel away parts of Nvidia's business.

"One of the things that we work very hard towards is trying to figure out how can we help there just be more compute in the world," OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman told reporters at a briefing in July.

OpenAI still relies on Nvidia chips for training, but has released its own chip for servicing AI queries and recently hired a compute executive, potentially indicating bigger ambitions.

Patrick Moorhead, CEO of Moor Insights, told Axios it would be a challenge but "it's possible" for OpenAI to compete with Nvidia, adding it took Google a decade to compete with Nvidia's chips strategy.

Zoom out: Nvidia currently owns the market for training AI models, according to Jay Goldberg, the lone Wall Street analyst with a sell rating on Nvidia.

There's a lot of training going on right now, but that could diminish over time if AI becomes commoditized and the performance gap between top-tier models shrinks.

In that world, demand for inference chips that are used to run AI models could outpace demand for training chips that Nvidia specializes in.

Nvidia "does not have a lock" on the inference market, and there are now dozens of competing chip offerings, Goldberg told Axios via email.

Case in point: Meta, Microsoft, Google and Amazon are all developing their own AI chips, though only Google and Amazon currently make them broadly available to customers through their cloud platforms.

"These companies believe that they can improve the total cost of ownership to run inference and in some cases training of the models," Moorhead said.

Reality check: Nvidia's customers repeatedly say they're not trying to compete with the chip giant.

Brockman believes "we will remain in this compute shortage no matter what," meaning there's room for more players to enter the space.

Nvidia also has CEO Jensen Huang's track record working for it.

The bottom line: Nvidia is financing customers that still need its most advanced chips today, while helping them reach the scale required to replace Nvidia in more of their workloads tomorrow.

text:
Dive Brief:

The two biggest players in the obesity and diabetes treatment market saw opposite reactions to their earnings reports this week, as Eli Lilly’s shares climbed and Novo Nordisk’s dropped.

Novo’s report Tuesday disappointed investors on two fronts. Its experimental CagriSema medicine failed to control blood sugar as well as Lilly’s tirzepatide in a head-to-head trial of patients with Type 2 diabetes. And Novo’s Wegovy pill, which has been a bright spot for the company, fell just short of analyst estimates for the second quarter.

Lilly, meanwhile, crushed Wall Street expectations with its results on Wednesday, RBC Capital Markets analyst Trung Huynh wrote in a note to clients. Second-quarter revenue jumped 48% to almost $23 billion, beating a consensus estimate of $20.6 billion. Lilly credited the continued growth of tirzepatide, the world’s best-selling drug, which is marketed as Mounjaro for diabetes and Zepbound for obesity.

Dive Insight:

Novo’s Ozempic, sold as Wegovy for obesity, was the first in the GLP-1 class of drugs to become a household name. But the company has steadily lost market share to Lilly, whose stock value has soared past the trillion-dollar mark.

The Danish drugmaker is trying to regain its footing with a new, higher-dose version of Wegovy and the oral formulation of the medicine. It has also touted the potential for CagriSema, a next-generation weekly injectable currently under Food and Drug Administration review. But CagriSema has delivered mixed results in studies, including the setback in the so-called Reimagine 4 trial announced Tuesday.

Meanwhile, Novo disappointed investors in the one area where it’s shown an edge in the obesity drug market, with its Wegovy pill. The drug got a head start on Lilly’s oral offering, Foundayo, and has had a faster launch. In the second quarter, the Wegovy pill had sales of 3.2 billion Danish kroner, or about $494 million, less than the 3.6 billion kroner expected by analysts. Novo’s shares fell 6% Tuesday before recovering some of their losses Wednesday.

Foundayo sales also fell short of Wall Street expectations in the quarter, coming in at $98 million versus a consensus estimate of $104 million, per RBC’s Huynh. But Lilly may be benefiting from lower expectations that are built in at this point for its pill. Certainly, investors were unperturbed by the report Wednesday, sending shares of the Indianapolis-based drugmaker 2% higher in early trading.

name: Adobe
title: How Agility Can Undermine Supply Chain Strategy
description:
Networks are now in a near‑permanent state of change as supplier lists balloon, lanes churn, and plan freezes evaporate.
In supply chains, agility is simply the ability to change course quickly when conditions change.
Where “always agile” breaks When agility becomes the operating system, not a tool, you see predictable side effects: ● Supplier and lane churn.
● Plan instability.
The literature links these “smart” supply chain foundations to better agility and resilience when they’re implemented with explicit constraints.
text:
Agility earned hero status early in the pandemic. Teams that could switch suppliers overnight, reroute freight on the fly, and rewrite production plans by the week kept goods moving. Five years on, and for many that reflex has hardened into the default operating mode. Networks are now in a near‑permanent state of change as supplier lists balloon, lanes churn, and plan freezes evaporate. Yet, service variance and costs stay stubbornly high. The paradox: agility, used everywhere all the time, is undermining resilience.

What does agility mean?

In supply chains, agility is simply the ability to change course quickly when conditions change. Conditions like shifting suppliers or nodes, rerouting freight, revising lot sizes, or re-prioritizing orders on short notice. Done selectively, agility improves responsiveness and, in many contexts, performance. But it was never meant to replace the slower, structural choices that keep a network steady most of the time. Research connects agility to responsiveness while cautioning that it is one capability among others, not a cure‑all.

A growing body of work also argues that high‑performing supply chains balance moving fast and building structure. This means they are treating agility as a targeted tool inside a broader design that includes flexibility, coordination, and resilience. Think of this as a deliberate balance rather than an “always sprint” culture.

Shocks and shifts

Not every disruption is the same.

● Shocks are sudden: a canal drought that throttles slots, a port closure after an accident, a new rule that takes effect overnight.

● Shifts are slower: energy prices trending up, eCommerce pulling demand into different nodes, production moving closer to customers.

Agility is the right tool for shocks; temporary moves that buy time. Shifts call for design choices: where to hold inventory, which lanes to anchor with capacity commitments, what contracts to put in place, and which suppliers to keep “warm” for specific risks. Research comparing supply chain strategies in the United States, France, and Poland during COVID-19 showed that outcomes improved when companies balanced fast response with structural measures.

Where “always agile” breaks

When agility becomes the operating system, not a tool, you see predictable side effects:

● Supplier and lane churn. Adding “just one more” backup feels safer, but sprawl dilutes leverage and increases onboarding debt. Quality noise creeps in while accountability blurs.

● Plan instability. Shrinking or ignoring freeze windows amplifies signal noise. Expedites become a habit, not an exception.

● Cost inflation masked as speed. Mode switches and premium freight lift unit economics; cash conversion worsens as inventory buffers ping‑pong.

● Tech that accelerates bad decisions. Digitized workflows can make you faster at changing the wrong things when thresholds and triggers are undefined.

● Novelty traps. Splashy “fast” tech (last‑mile drones) may help in narrow use cases, but without network redesign, they often raise the total cost‑to‑serve. Systematic reviews emphasize boundary conditions and trade‑offs.

6 steps to a sturdy playbook: Agility and structure

If “set guardrails” sounds vague, here’s what it looks like in practice:

1. Clear switching triggers

Define the conditions that justify moving to a backup: delay beyond X days, defect rate above Y%, capacity utilization above Z% for N weeks, or a specific regulatory change. Make these thresholds visible in your control tower and S&OP so a switch is a measured response, not a reflex.

2. Pre‑arranged backups

Keep alternate suppliers, DCs, and lanes commercially “warm” with pricing, service terms, data connections, and SOPs already in place. The point isn’t to use them weekly; it’s to activate them cleanly when a trigger fires. Recent work frames these as dynamic capabilities: options you can switch to quickly without re‑inventing governance in a crisis.

3. Variability‑sized buffers

Hold safety stock or introduce hold points where variability is highest, sized to forecast error and replenishment time, not to averages. This absorbs routine turbulence, so frontline teams don’t need to re‑plan constantly.

4. Freeze windows with exceptions

Protect a stable plan horizon by product family or market, then budget a small, visible “exception pool” for the genuine surprises. This reduces noise while preserving room to act when it truly matters.

5. Rapid‑activation facilities

Designate sites you can light up quickly after an interruption. These should include layouts, labor playbooks, carrier appointments, and pre-built data integrations. The goal is to activate within hours or days, not weeks.

6. Digital enablement with constraints

Let the system do the boring parts: surface when triggers are met, release pre‑approved playbooks, route orders to the best available node, and document the cost‑of‑change. Digitalization can connect purchasing, fulfillment, and transportation so that agility occurs within established rules. The literature links these “smart” supply chain foundations to better agility and resilience when they’re implemented with explicit constraints.

This is the balance the research points toward: agility as a targeted, condition‑based response nested in a network built for steadiness, flexibility, coordination, and resilience working together rather than competing for attention.

Noting the cost of change

Most companies track service and unit cost; fewer track the cost of churn created by constant pivots. Instead, make it visible:

● Supplier onboarding cycle time and re‑onboarding frequency

● Plan‑freeze adherence

● Expedite percentage and spend

● Lane churn rate

● Slow‑moving and obsolete inventory growth versus demand volatility

If those curves are rising while the external environment is relatively stable, agility isn’t protecting you. It’s eroding your economics. The academic record ties agility to performance gains when it’s part of a coherent capability set; measuring the cost‑of‑change helps ensure it stays that way.

Your agility self-checklist

Five questions to ask before the next “urgent” pivot:

How many of our last 20 expedites were tied to a documented trigger vs. a gut call?

Is our supplier count up while OTIF is flat?

Are freeze‑window breaches climbing month over month?

Are we changing lanes/modes faster than demand is actually moving?

Did our latest tech rollout include explicit switching thresholds or just speed?

If the answers point to churn, you’re practicing agility without structure. That’s not resilience; it’s burnout with better software. Organizations fared better when rapid moves were paired with routines and capacities that could be activated quickly without major re-wiring.

The bottom line
